concepts.angle: The pupil's own exam script, written in advance over two years. The speaking exam draws on 270 known questions (questions.json: 113 begin "Cad", 70 are yes/no "An" questions, 203 address the pupil directly with tú, agat, leat or ort), and it rewards prepared personal answers. So the app is not a drill with an exam skin; it is the script itself. It holds 270 numbered lines, one per question, on 12 topic pages. A line is the pupil's own answer, typed on the ruled lines in biro, marked in the margin in the principal's red hand, recorded once in the pupil's voice, and then rewritten from memory at widening intervals until it is theirs. Everything else in the app (the recall trainer, the grammar engine, the word index) exists only to make the next line possible or the last line better, and every item says in the margin which line it belongs to. The answer key for recall is the pupil's own earlier writing, which is the one thing that exists today without authored model answers. By exam day nothing is said or written for the first time.
concepts.workingTitle: Suggestion only: "Mo Scríbhinn" (my script: the pupil's own exam script, written before the exam). "Cuimhne" names a means; this names the end. "An Scríbhinn" would also do.
concepts.purpose: Write your exam answers now, a line a night, so on the day you have said it all before.
concepts.promise: About twenty school nights, so about twenty written pages and twenty lines of the script: the whole first topic page (the 21 "Myself, my family" questions, Q001 to Q021) and the start of the next, each line in the pupil's own words, each rewritten from memory at least twice and marked against their own earlier line, each recorded once in their own voice. The 60 to 80 listed words those lines use are ticked as known in the index; the article and preposition forms of the nouns in those lines (ar an bhord, sa charr, leis an mhúinteoir) have been drilled from their own sentences. They can answer any of those 21 questions aloud without notes. And they can print the page and hand it to their teacher, so the teacher marks a script that already exists. Before, they had a list of words and no answers; after, they have one twelfth of their exam written.
concepts.forWhom: Pupils at St Paul's learning Irish, Years 8 to 12. The 270 questions are the Year 11 and 12 pupils' own exam, so they are the first audience. Years 8 to 10 open the same script from page 1 (the "Mé féin" context: 86 questions across four topics) with the Key Stage 3 frequency list as their word spine (826 entries, gender and part of speech given) and write one-sentence lines; a Year 11 rewrites the same line as three sentences with an opinion and a reason. Within that, pupils with ADD and ADHD are served first: the whole thing is one page a night, fixed order, five minutes, marked as it goes, and the progress is a physical object filling up rather than a percentage.

thread.idea: The script. The app is a single exam booklet belonging to one candidate: a cover, twelve topic pages of numbered lines (270 in all), an index of words at the back, and a date-stamped daily page on which tonight's work is done. The pupil is a candidate from the first night, not a learner playing a game. Every screen is a page of that booklet and every task on it is traceable to a line of the script.
thread.onEveryScreen: Five fixed things. (1) The candidate box at the top of every screen carries the same four cells and never a score: Ainm, Rang, the sitting (Scrúdú: Bealtaine 2028, from the exam date in settings) and the script count (Líne 38 de 270). The page number sits top right as on a printed booklet. (2) Under the box, one italic rubric line in the exam's own form of words with a grey English gloss (the existing Rubric component); this is the line that says what the screen is for, and it is the only heading. (3) Every item on any screen prints its line reference in the margin in small print (L38 beside the word clár, L12 beside a grammar form), so the pupil can always see why they are being asked. (4) The pupil's own words are always in biro blue on ruled lines, wherever they are quoted; set text is in the print face; marks are only ever in the red hand in the margin: ticks, crossings-out, corrections, and short comments (fada!, séimhiú de dhíth, cad chuige?). Never a number, never a percentage. (5) The foot of every screen has one action. There is no tab bar; the booklet's other pages are reached from a contents line on the cover in plain print (An scríbhinn · Innéacs · Scrúdú béil) and from the line references themselves.
thread.whyNotGeneric: No general language app holds the 270 questions this pupil's examiner will actually ask, in the school's own dialect, marked in the handwriting of their own principal in the red pen they see on their marked jotters. No general app can use the pupil's own earlier answer as the answer key, because it has no reason to keep a script. And no general app ends in an object: this one ends in a booklet the pupil can print and hand to a teacher, and carry in their head into the exam room.

firstRun.ga: Seo do scríbhinn féin. Gach oíche, scríobhfaidh tú líne amháin: d'fhreagra féin ar cheist a chuirfeas an scrúdaitheoir ort. Marcálfaidh mé é sa chiumhais, le peann dearg. Faoi lá an scrúdaithe ní bheidh rud ar bith á rá agat den chéad uair. Cúig bhomaite san oíche, sin an méid.
firstRun.en: This is your own exam script. Every night you write one line: your own answer to a question the examiner will ask. I mark it in the margin in red pen. By exam day nothing you say will be for the first time. Five minutes a night, that is all.

home.headline: Do scrúdú, scríofa agat roimh ré. (Your exam, written by you in advance.) Set as the rubric line under the candidate box; it is the purpose of the app and it is on the first screen every night.
home.shows: Three things, all on one ruled page. (1) Tonight's page: the page number and date (Lch. 41 · Dé Máirt 29 Meán Fómhair) and, on the first ruled lines, the question that is tonight's new line (Líne 38. Cad é an clár teilifíse is fearr leat?) with the lines beneath it blank. The pupil sees the actual work before they start, and it is one question. (2) The state of the script, in the candidate box: Líne 37 de 270 and the sitting. Nothing else numeric. For a Year 8 the denominator is the open context (de 86). (3) Last night's marking, in the red hand in the margin beside the page: 5 ticks and the one correction written out (sa charr), so the pupil sees what to fix before it comes round again in tonight's rewrite. Why those three: what I do now, how far the script has got, what I got wrong last time. Streaks, due counts and learned totals are cut; they are counters about the app, not about the script. The contents line at the foot (An scríbhinn · Innéacs · Scrúdú béil) is plain print, as on a paper's contents.
home.singleAction: Scríobh an leathanach (Write the page). One button, the only one on the screen.

structure.purposeLine: Do scrúdú, scríofa agat roimh ré. (Your exam, written by you in advance.)
structure.content: Candidate box (Ainm, Rang, Scrúdú: Bealtaine 2028, Líne 37 de 270). Tonight's page number and date. Tonight's new question on the ruled lines. Last night's marks in the margin. One button: Scríobh an leathanach. A contents line in print at the foot: An scríbhinn · Innéacs · Scrúdú béil · Clúdach istigh.

structure.screen: Leathanach an lae (today's page; the five-minute session)
structure.purposeLine: Cúig bhomaite. Líne amháin eile ar do scríbhinn. (Five minutes. One more line on your script.)
structure.content: One ruled page filled top to bottom in a fixed order, the same every night, one item live at a time with finished items marked above it. Item 1 Athscríobh: a due line from the script, question shown, the pupil's own earlier answer hidden; rewritten from memory; marked word by word against their own saved line (ticks over matching words, missing or misspelt words written in red in the margin, fada! for a fada slip). Items 2 to 4 Focail: three words, English given, Irish typed, verbs asking root and verbal noun in two boxes as now (343 GCSE verbs carry a verbal noun); chosen in this order: words marked red in item 1, then words from the current topic's list that have not yet appeared in any of the pupil's lines, then due words; each carries its line reference in the margin; a wrong word comes round again at the foot of the page. Item 5 Foirm amháin: one article or preposition-plus-article form generated from a noun in last night's or tonight's line, diagnosed by rule as in Grammar.swift (urú, ní séimhiú!). Item 6 Líne nua: the next unwritten question on the current page; one to three sentences on the ruled lines; a word bank printed in the exam's manner at the foot of the page (is maith liom · ní maith liom · is fearr liom · mar · fosta, drawn from the 27 entries of the opinions group and the connectives group) that inserts on tap; marking: ticks on listed words, ? on words not on any list (never a cross), mutation rules checked by pattern where the noun's gender is known, and cad chuige? in the margin when an opinion has no mar after it; then Abair é: record once, play back. Close: the page is stamped with the date in the hand, the marks summarised as ticks and corrections in words (5 thic, 1 cheartú), Sin é anocht, and a small print link Leathanach eile for anyone who wants more.

structure.purposeLine: Gach a ndéarfaidh tú ar lá an scrúdaithe, i do chuid focal féin. (Everything you will say on the day, in your own words.)
structure.content: Twelve topic pages in the order of the three contexts (Mé féin 86 questions, Saol na scoile agus saol na hoibre 91, Mo cheantar 93). Each page is the topic's questions as numbered lines: an unwritten line is a blank rule, a written line is in biro, the margin carries its red marks and a small date, and a line that has been recorded shows a small print mark (taifeadta). Page header: Líne 12 de 21 scríofa. Tap a line to open it. A page with every line written gets Críochnaithe in the hand across the top. Foot of each page: Priontáil an leathanach, which produces an A4 PDF of the page with the candidate box, so the teacher marks by hand on paper the way they mark now.

structure.purposeLine: Freagra amháin. Do chuidse. Ní bheidh ort é a chumadh ar an lá. (One answer. Yours. You will not have to make it up on the day.)
structure.content: The question in italic as the rubric. The pupil's answer on ruled lines in biro, fada keys above the keyboard. Word bank at the foot in print. Seiceáil marks as on the daily page. Abair é records and plays back; the recording is kept with the line. Earlier drafts listed beneath as Dréacht 1, 14 Meán Fómhair, crossed through, so the pupil sees the line grow from one sentence in Year 8 to three in Year 11. Athscríobh ó chuimhne link to rewrite it now. A word marked ? can be tapped and added to Mo chuid focal féin (the pupil's personal vocabulary) with its English, and then enters the recall rounds; this is the Key Stage 3 framework's small personal vocabulary.

structure.screen: Innéacs (the word index at the back of the booklet)
structure.purposeLine: Na focail atá de dhíth ar do scríbhinn, agus cé acu atá agat. (The words your script needs, and which ones you have.)
structure.content: One list per topic page (GCSE: the topic groups, e.g. Caitheamh aimsire 316; Key Stage 3: the frequency bands, Na 100 focal is coitianta first). Each word shows, in the hand, a tick if it has been written correctly in a line and recalled, ? if attempted, nothing if never met; gender printed after nouns where known (fir., bain.). Tap a word to see the line of the script it appears in. Cleachtaigh na focail seo starts a page of five words from this list only. Mo chuid focal féin is the last list.

structure.purposeLine: Mar a bheas sé ar an lá: ceist gan choinne, gan do scríbhinn os do chomhair. (As it will be on the day: a question you did not expect, without your script in front of you.)
structure.content: Offered only once a topic page has ten written lines. Five questions drawn at random from written pages. The question is shown in print (heard aloud only when Abair arrives), a countdown runs (the only timer in the app), the pupil answers aloud and it records. After each, the pupil's own written line is revealed under the recording and they mark themselves with one tap: a tick, or arís, which sends the line back to box 0. Ends with the five marks in the margin and the recordings kept.

structure.purposeLine: Cé thú féin agus cá huair a bheas an scrúdú. (Who you are and when the exam is.)
structure.content: Name, class, stage (Eochairchéim 3 or GCSE), exam month and year. The exam date sets the pace: unwritten lines divided by school nights left gives lines per night, shown on the cover when it rises above one. Strict fadas on or off. Words per page (three by default, five at most). Priontáil an scríbhinn ar fad. Glan an scríbhinn, with a warning, since the script is two years of work.

concepts.dailyLoop: Open the app. The cover shows tonight's page number, the date, and the question that will be tonight's new line. Tap Scríobh an leathanach. Step 1, about a minute: Athscríobh. A due line from the script comes up (L12, Cá mhéad deartháir atá agat?, written nine days ago); the earlier answer is hidden; the pupil writes it again from memory. Seiceáil: ticks appear over each word that matches their own saved line, the missing word is written in red in the margin, a wrong fada gets fada!. Step 2, about ninety seconds: three words, one at a time. First the word they missed in step 1, then a word from the topic list they have not yet used in any line, then a due word. English shown, Irish typed, verbs in two boxes. Marked instantly; a wrong one is queued again for the foot of the page. Step 3, about forty-five seconds: one grammar form from a noun in their own line (ar an + bord), marked and diagnosed by rule. Step 4, about ninety seconds: Líne nua. The next unwritten question on the current page (Q040, An maith leat an teilifís?). They write one to three sentences; the word bank at the foot offers is maith liom, ní maith liom, mar, fosta. Seiceáil ticks the listed words, puts ? beside anything not on the list, checks the mutations it can, and writes cad chuige? in the margin if there is an opinion with no reason. They tap Abair é and say the line once into the phone, then hear it back. Step 5, fifteen seconds: any word queued from step 2 is asked once more; the page is stamped with the date; Sin é anocht. Feicfidh mé amárach thú. The cover now reads Líne 38 de 270. Total about five minutes; nothing else is offered unless they tap the small Leathanach eile.
concepts.register: Keep it, and make it literal. Under this angle the exam script is not a visual register laid over a drill; it is the data structure. A page is a page, a line is a line, a mark is a mark. The register was failing in the proof of concept because it was decorating things that are not script: statistics written on copybook lines (3 focal ar eolas, 2 lá as a chéile), invented unit labels (Aonad 1 · Cuimhne, Aonad 3 · Gramadach), numeric scores in the candidate box (11/11, 3/4) which also breach the ruling that this is a practice booklet not a test, and an example sentence in the mock-up (Sampla: Buailim le mo chairde) for which no data exists. What it must do on each screen: the candidate box must carry the pupil's real standing (name, class, sitting, line count) and nothing that is a score; the rubric line must be the one heading and must say what the screen is for; the ruled lines must only ever carry the pupil's own words in biro, so if a screen has ruled lines and nobody writes on them the screen is wrong; the margin must carry marks in the hand and line references in print and nothing else; the page number and date stamp must be real and must accumulate; and the foot must carry one action. The test for any new screen: could this page be printed and handed to a teacher and make sense as a page of a candidate's script. The cover, the script, a line and the index all pass; a tab bar, a settings list and a streak do not, which is why they go.
concepts.adhd: The script serves this fork better than the drill did because progress is an object, not a number: pages fill, lines appear in biro, a topic page gets Críochnaithe written across it. Specifics carried into the design: the daily page has the same six items in the same order every night, so there is nothing to decide; only one item is live on the screen at a time and the completed ones sit marked above it; the default is three words, not five, and never a queue shown up front; every item is marked the instant Seiceáil is tapped, in the margin, in the hand; a word got wrong is asked again at the foot of the same page (a re-test inside one session), and a new line written tonight is asked again as tomorrow's rewrite; the spacing boxes are shortened from the proof of concept's 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 30 days to 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 so nothing disappears for a month; the page closes itself after five minutes with Sin é anocht and does not offer more unless asked; there is no timer anywhere except the cold exam, which the pupil chooses; and the print face is Atkinson Hyperlegible at 20 point for anything the pupil must read or type, one question per screen. The cover shows last night's correction so the day begins with one known thing to fix, which is the kind of concrete, near-term target these pupils can hold.
cuts: The five-tab bar (Inniu, Innéacs, Gramadach, Labhairt, Socruithe): a generic app shell and the thing the principal rejected first time; replaced by a cover with a contents line.
The Home screen's streak, due count, learned count and sessions-today written on copybook lines: statistics about the app dressed as script; replaced by page, line count and last night's marks.
Numeric scores in the candidate box (11/11, 3/4, marksSoFar in SessionView and GrammarView): breach the practice-booklet ruling; only ticks and corrections remain.
The invented unit labels Aonad 1 · Cuimhne, Aonad 2 · Labhairt, Aonad 3 · Gramadach: they name nothing in any exam; the rubric line takes their place.
The Gramadach tab as a free-standing drill on random nouns from the whole list: grammar now draws its noun from the pupil's own lines and appears as one item on the daily page.

The default of gender m for unmarked nouns (noun.gender ?? "m" in Grammar.swift): the GCSE list has 827 nouns marked masculine and none marked feminine, so unmarked feminine nouns would be drilled as masculine (an fuinneog). Grammar draws only on nouns with a known gender (the 362 Key Stage 3 nouns) until the workbook cleaning pass marks the GCSE list.
The Labhairt three-level list (topics, then questions, then a question) as the way into speaking: replaced by the script's pages, where every question is already a line.
The Innéacs tab with a learned count per topic as a primary destination: becomes the index at the back of the booklet, showing which words have appeared in the script.
The mock-up's Sampla sentence under a recall item: no example sentences exist in the data and none should be shown until authored and checked.
Sessions of 24 questions (Ceist 12 de 24 in the mock-up) and the 30-day top spacing interval: replaced by three words per page and boxes of 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 days.
Socruithe as a tab: becomes the inside cover, reached from the contents line, and gains the exam date which the app needs to pace the script.
The app name Cuimhne, if the angle is adopted: it names a means, not the script.
risks: No model answers exist, so the app cannot judge whether a line is good Irish; it can only tick listed words, flag fadas, check the mutation rules the engine knows, and prompt for structure. A pupil could rehearse a wrong sentence for two years. Mitigation in the concept is the printed page for the teacher to mark by hand; a real fix needs either authored model answers checked by an Irish teacher or a teacher view (direction E), neither of which exists.

Word-level marking of free text needs the pupil's words matched to headwords through initial mutations and inflection. The mutation engine handles séimhiú, urú and t- but nothing of plurals or the genitive, so ticks will be missed. The rule must be that an unmatched word gets ? and never a cross.

The 270 questions carry no English gloss and no audio. A Year 8 may not understand a question; a gloss for each question is a small authoring task (an evening) but must be done and checked. Hearing the question is what happens in the exam; until the Abair Ulster voice is integrated the cold exam shows the question in print, which is half the exam.

Speech is recorded but never marked; there is no Irish speech recognition on the device. Self-marking against the pupil's own written line is honest but weak. Abair's recognition is the only route and is untested for this age group and dialect.

Phonics (the 62 sound-symbol correspondences) and the Key Stage 3 hear-and-type work are not in this concept because they need audio; they wait for Abair, which pushes it earlier in the build order than the proposal had it.

Questions map to vocabulary only at topic level and the topic names differ between the two files (Free time, leisure and daily routine against Caitheamh aimsire and Dialann an lae), so a twelve-row hand table is needed; the words a given line needs are not known in advance and are derived only from what the pupil writes or has not yet used.

The Key Stage 3 framework wants unprepared speech; a prepared script could be read as the opposite. The cold exam and the rewrite-from-memory are the unprepared parts and need to be visible enough that the app is not seen as rote learning of set answers.

Pacing depends on an exam date the pupil or teacher must enter. A Year 12 who starts in February has 270 lines and perhaps 60 school nights, so the app must show lines per night honestly rather than pretend one a night still works.

The lines are personal (family, home, part-time job, plans). They stay on the device in the concept, but a printed page leaves the device and any later sync (iCloud, a teacher view) is a safeguarding and data question for the school before it is built.

The rubric wording, the topic names and the 270 questions are the examining body's material. The app must not print rubrics verbatim in a way that identifies the board, and distribution beyond the school remains the permissions question already logged.

The marking hand is a digitised sample; whether it contains the tick, cross and question mark glyphs used everywhere here, and Irish accented capitals, must be checked against the font proof before any screen relies on them.

The GCSE list is uncleaned (14 broken entries, feminine gender unmarked, sub-heading bleed); the index and the grammar item will expose those faults to pupils directly, so the workbook cleaning pass is a precondition, not a nicety.

concepts.angle: Five minutes a night, no more, built first for the pupil with ADHD. Attention is the design constraint, not content. The whole app is one small task, "do your page", done once a night; everything else in the proof of concept (the index, the grammar drill, the speaking browser, the settings tab) is either folded into that one page or pushed behind it, reachable only by turning back through the copybook. There is no home screen separate from the task, no start button, no tab bar, no counter, no streak, no timer. Opening the app is starting; closing the marked page is finishing.
concepts.workingTitle: Suggestion only: "Cóipleabhar" (the copybook: one page filled every night, marked in red before it is closed). Alternative if a shorter word is wanted: "Leathanach" (the page). The proof of concept's name "Cuimhne" is not wrong, but it names the aim; "Cóipleabhar" names the thing the pupil holds, which is what runs through every screen.
concepts.purpose: One page of Irish a night, five minutes, marked in red before you close it, so the words stick.
concepts.promise: A numbered pile of marked pages, about 28 if they missed none, that they can turn back through. On those pages: roughly 50 to 60 distinct words from the school's list, each written from memory two to four times with the fada in the right place, not 300 words glanced at once; about 28 article and preposition forms in the Ulster shape (an fhuinneog, ar an bhord, sa charr) each produced, marked, and rewritten if wrong; and, at GCSE stage, their own written answers to around 20 of the 270 questions the examiner actually asks, each one recalled from memory at least once and now sitting at the back of the copybook as a personal answer bank for the speaking exam. Plus the thing that matters most for this pupil: the habit of a five-minute task that has never once been a chore longer than five minutes, and that has never punished a missed night.
concepts.forWhom: Pupils in Years 8 to 12 at St Paul's learning Irish, designed first for the pupil with ADD or ADHD who will not sit through a twenty-minute app, who abandons anything once a streak breaks, and who needs to see the mark the moment the answer is written. Year 8 to 10 work from the Key Stage 3 frequency spine (826 entries); Year 11 and 12 from the GCSE topic spine (2,233 entries) and the 270 examiner questions. The class number typed into the candidate box on the first night chooses the spine; the pupil never sees the word "stage". The teacher is not a user of this version; a teacher view is listed under risks, not assumed.

thread.idea: The copybook. Every night one page is written, from the top line down, and marked in red in the margin as each line is finished. A wrong line is written out again at the foot under "Ceartúcháin", the way corrections go in a real copybook. The page is then closed and numbered. Nothing exists in the app that is not a page of this one copybook: tonight's page at the front, the marked pages behind it, the pupil's own words and answers at the back, name and class on the cover.
thread.onEveryScreen: Every screen is a page of the same copybook and carries the same four things in the same places. (1) The candidate box at the top: Ainm, Rang, and the page number in the pen hand (Leathanach 12), never a score, never a question counter. (2) Under the box, one line in italic that says what this page is for, in Irish with a grey English gloss, the same wording every night. (3) The ruled lines with the red margin: one line is one item, lines fill from the top, the empty lines below are the only progress indicator the pupil needs, and the red margin is where the tick, the cross or the correction goes the moment a line is checked. (4) The pen hand at the foot: the comment on tonight's page, the pupil's own words at the back, the note on the closed page saying what comes back tomorrow. Navigation is turning pages, not tabs: swipe back to see earlier marked pages, keep going to reach the back of the book. Tonight's page is where the app opens and where it returns.
thread.whyNotGeneric: It is a St Paul's copybook marked in the principal's own digitised hand with the school's red pen. The corrections are Ulster forms (ar an bhord, not ar an mbord; cad é, fosta, madadh) generated by the school's own rule engine from the gender tags in the school's list, which no shop app does. The question line draws on the exact 270 questions the examiner will ask, and the model answer for each is the pupil's own previous answer, so the copybook becomes theirs: no two copybooks in the school hold the same page 20. And the frame is a practice booklet, not a test: ticks and corrections, no percentages, no timer, which is the opposite of what a generic language app measures.

firstRun.ga: Seo do chóipleabhar. Leathanach amháin achan oíche, cúig nóiméad, sin an méid. Scríobh na focail agus ceartóidh mise iad le peann dearg ar an chiumhais. Rud ar bith atá contráilte anocht, tiocfaidh sé ar ais amárach. Cad é an t-ainm atá ort?
firstRun.en: This is your copybook. One page every night, five minutes, that is all. Write the words and I will mark them in red in the margin. Anything wrong tonight comes back tomorrow. What is your name?

home.headline: There is no home screen distinct from the task. The app opens onto tonight's page. The candidate box reads Leathanach 12 in the pen hand with the date beside it (Dé Máirt 29 Meán Fómhair), and the line under the box, the same every night, reads: Leathanach amháin. Cúig nóiméad. (One page. Five minutes.)
home.shows: Three things and nothing else. First, the candidate box: name and class in biro blue, the page number in red, and the page number is the only long-term measure in the whole app; it counts pages done, it never resets, and a missed night simply does not add a page. Second, the ruled page with its five empty lines, where line 1 is already live: the English prompt is written on it ("the window"), the answer box is on the same line, the cursor is in it and the keyboard is up with the fada row above it. The four blank lines beneath show, without a counter, how much is left. Third, in the margin at the top, a short note carried over from last night in the pen hand: "ó aréir: fuinneog" (from last night: window), so the pupil knows one of tonight's lines is the one they got wrong. Nothing about totals, due counts, learned counts or sessions today: those numbers from the current HomeView are exactly what a pupil with ADHD reads as a queue, and a queue is what makes them close the app.
home.singleAction: Write on line 1. There is no Tosaigh button; opening the app is starting. Return or Seiceáil marks the line and opens line 2.

structure.screen: An chéad leathanach (first run, seen once)
structure.purposeLine: Seo do chóipleabhar. (This is your copybook.)
structure.content: The first-run speech above, set in the print face on the ruled lines. Under it the candidate box with two blanks, Ainm and Rang, which the pupil fills in biro blue. The class number chooses the spine silently: 8, 9 or 10 gives the Key Stage 3 frequency list; 11 or 12 gives the GCSE topic list and the 270 questions. No tour, no permissions prompt, no other setting. As soon as Rang is filled, line 1 of page 1 opens on the next screen. The notification permission is asked for on the second night, not the first, with the words "Cuirfidh mé i gcuimhne duit ag a hocht" (I will remind you at eight).

structure.purposeLine: Leathanach amháin. Cúig nóiméad. (One page. Five minutes.)
structure.content: Five ruled lines in a fixed order that never changes, so every night looks like the last. Lines 1 to 3, words: English on the line, Irish written in the box on the same line; one of the three is new (a small grey "nua" beside it), the others are due for revisit, with last night's wrong word always first. A verb line takes root and verbal noun on the one line (buail le / ag bualadh le), as the data supplies for 343 GCSE verbs. Line 4, grammar: the pieces shown ("ar an + bord", "an + fuinneog") and the pupil writes the joined form; marked by the rule engine, and a wrong answer gets the diagnosis in the hand ("urú, ní séimhiú!", "t- de dhíth"). This line draws only on the 362 Key Stage 3 nouns that carry a gender tag (246 masculine, 116 feminine), because the GCSE list carries 827 masculine marks and not one feminine mark, so it cannot be trusted for this until cleaned. Line 5, the sentence: at GCSE stage one of the 270 examiner questions is written on the line ("Cad é an t-ábhar is fearr leat?") and the pupil writes one sentence in answer. The first time, they are authoring: the pen marks what it can prove (a known word without its fada, a known noun unlenited after a known preposition and article) and ticks the line as written. Every later time that question comes round, the line shows the question only and the pupil writes their answer from memory; their own earlier sentence is the model, and the pen underlines what is missing or changed. At Key Stage 3 the fifth line is "Scríobh abairt leis an fhocal seo" with one of tonight's words, marked the same way. Only one line is live at a time; finished lines sit above, marked; unwritten lines are blank rule. "Taispeáin dom" is a small grey link on the live line; using it writes the answer in red and sends the line to the corrections. After a stall of about 45 seconds with nothing typed, the pen writes the first letter of the answer on the line as a hint, which counts as a correction. Beneath the five lines, under a short heading "Ceartúcháin" in the hand, any wrong line is written out again by the pupil before the page can close: this is the in-session retest and it is in register. Then the pen writes one short comment ("maith thú", "fada ar ó!", "fuinneog arís amárach") and one button appears: Dún (Close).

structure.screen: An leathanach ceartaithe (the closed page, what the pupil sees on reopening the same night)
structure.purposeLine: Ceartaithe. Amárach arís. (Marked. Again tomorrow.)
structure.content: The same page, now read-only: the ticks and crosses in the margin, the corrections at the foot, the comment, and a margin note in the hand of what comes back tomorrow ("amárach: fuinneog, ar an bhord"). No score, no summary screen; the marked page is the result. One small grey link at the foot: "Leathanach eile?" (Another page?), which opens a second page of the same shape from the same queue. It is never shown before tonight's page is done, and it is a link, not a button, so that continuing is offered and not asked for. Reopening the app on a finished night lands here, not on a new page.

structure.screen: Na leathanaigh roimhe (the previous pages, swipe back from tonight)
structure.purposeLine: Gach leathanach a rinne tú. (Every page you have done.)
structure.content: The earlier marked pages, newest first, each exactly as it was closed, with its number and date in the candidate box. Nothing is summarised, charted or totalled. Missed nights do not appear as blank pages; the numbers simply run 11, 12, 13 across whatever dates they fell on. This is the whole progress view, and it is the pile of pages itself, which is the thing a pupil with ADHD can actually feel.

structure.screen: Cúl an chóipleabhair: Mo chuid focal (the back of the book, keep swiping)
structure.purposeLine: Do chuid focal féin. Tiocfaidh siad ar leathanach. (Your own words. They will come up on a page.)
structure.content: Ruled lines where the pupil adds their own words, English beside Irish: their surname, their townland, their club, the dog's name, the words the Key Stage 3 appendix leaves as placeholders for a placename and the pupil's surname. Each entry joins the queue as a new word and appears on a night's page like any other. At GCSE stage a second section, Mo chuid freagraí (My answers), lists every examiner question the pupil has answered on a line 5, with their current answer under it in biro blue; this is the personal answer bank they read the night before the speaking exam. A small grey count (18 de 270) is allowed here and nowhere else, because here the pupil has chosen to look.

structure.screen: An clúdach (the cover, reached only by tapping the candidate box)
structure.purposeLine: Ainm, rang, agus sin é. (Name, class, and that is it.)
structure.content: Name, class (which changes the spine), the reminder time, a strict-fadas switch for Higher tier, and "Glan an cóipleabhar" behind a confirmation. No questions-per-round setting: the page is five lines and that is the design. No stage picker: class decides.

concepts.dailyLoop:
1. At eight o'clock one notification, the same words every night: "Do leathanach." The pupil opens the app. Tonight's page is already open, dated, numbered, line 1 live, keyboard up, fada row above it. (0:00)
2. Line 1, the word from last night: "the window". They type "fuinneog" and press return. A red tick lands in the margin at once. Line 2 opens. (0:40)
3. Lines 2 and 3, one new and one revisit: "(to) meet (someone)" wants "buail le" and "ag bualadh le" on the one line; "the town" wants "baile". On line 3 they type "bailé". The pen strikes it, writes "baile" above in red, and a cross goes in the margin. "baile" is written as a heading under Ceartúcháin at the foot. (2:00)
4. Line 4, grammar: "ar an + bord". They type "ar an mbord". Cross in the margin, "bhord" in red above, and the diagnosis in the hand: "urú, ní séimhiú!" with the one-line rule under it in grey. "ar an bhord" goes to the corrections. (2:50)
5. Line 5, the question: "Cad é an t-ábhar is fearr leat?" Second time they have met it, so they write their own answer from memory: "Is fearr liom Gaeilge mar tá an múinteoir go maith." Their answer from page 6 is the model; the pen underlines nothing missing and ticks it. (4:00)
6. Ceartúcháin: they write "baile" and "ar an bhord" once each on the two correction lines. Both ticked. (4:40)
7. The pen writes "maith thú, baile arís amárach" at the foot. They tap Dún. The candidate box now reads Leathanach 13. Under it, small and grey, "Leathanach eile?" They close the app. (5:00)
concepts.register: Keep it. It is not decoration here; it is the mechanism. The copybook page gives the app its one-thing-at-a-time structure (one line is one item), its progress indicator (empty lines below the live one), its in-session retest (Ceartúcháin at the foot), its feedback (the mark in the margin, in the principal's hand, in the school's red), and its record (the pile of marked pages). Remove the register and every one of those needs a generic substitute: a progress bar, a results card, a stats tab, which is the "designed by AI" mock-up that was rejected. Three changes to how the proof of concept uses it, so that it serves rather than decorates. First, the candidate box carries name, class and page number only; the running fraction (11/11) and the counter (Ceist 12 de 24) go, because they are test signals and a queue, and the proposal's own ruling was ticks and corrections, no percentages. Second, the unit labels (Aonad 1 · Cuimhne, Aonad 3 · Gramadach) go; there are no units, there is one page. Third, the italic rubric line becomes the purpose line: on tonight's page it is always "Leathanach amháin. Cúig nóiméad." and the exam papers' own wording (Scríobh an focal ceart sa bhosca) appears only as a grey gloss on the live line, where the task really is the exam task. What the register must do on each screen: the ruled line must be the unit of work and of marking, never a card; the red margin must carry a mark for every finished line, never a summary elsewhere; the pen hand must appear only for marking, correcting, page numbers and the closing comment, never for headings or navigation, or it stops reading as a teacher's pen; and the print face (Atkinson Hyperlegible, as in the mock-up; the proof of concept fell back to the system font) must be large and single-weight, because the pupil this is for reads better with one face at one size.
concepts.adhd: Every decision above is the ADHD fork carried through, so this lists only what changes against the proof of concept. One live line at a time, with finished lines locked above and blank rule below, so there is never a second thing to attend to; the proof of concept already shows one question per screen, but around it are a counter, a score and a tab bar, all of which compete. Immediate marking: the mark lands the instant a line is checked, on the same screen, in the margin, not on a results screen afterwards. Visible progress in minutes: the page filling down is the progress, and the page number goes up at the close. Fixed shape: five lines in the same order every night, word, word, word, grammar, sentence, then corrections, then the comment, then Dún; a pupil who has done page 3 knows page 30 by heart. Short by design, not by setting: the questions-per-round setting goes, the page is five lines, and a second page is an offered link after the first, never a queue shown before it. Shorter spacing: intervals 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 days rather than the proof of concept's 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 30, and a word wrong tonight is always line 1 tomorrow, so the pupil meets their mistake before they can dread it. In-session retest in register: a wrong line is rewritten at the foot before the page closes. No streak: the proof of concept counts "lá as a chéile", and a broken streak is the moment this pupil deletes an app; page numbers never go backwards. No timer, ever, and no cold exam mode on the nightly page. No numbers about the future: no due count, no learned-out-of-2,233, nothing that reads as how far behind they are. Stall handling: after about 45 seconds of nothing typed, the pen gives the first letter rather than leaving the pupil stuck or reaching for the reveal. One notification, at a time the pupil chose, with the same two words every night. Keyboard already up on open, fada row fixed above it, so there is no first tap to find. Large single-weight type, high contrast on the paper colour, no grey-on-grey. Ask for notification permission on the second night, not the first, so the first run is one screen and one question.
cuts: The five-tab bar (Inniu, Innéacs, Gramadach, Labhairt, Socruithe) and the RootView TabView; navigation becomes page-turning.
The Innéacs tab (IndexView): browsing every topic or frequency band with learned counts. The pupil's only view of the list is the words that reach their page and the back-of-book pages.
Gramadach as a separate open-ended drill (GrammarView with its own running score). The rule engine stays and becomes line 4 of every page.

Labhairt as a browsable bank of 270 questions by topic with a recorder (SpeakingView, TopicQuestionsView, QuestionView). The questions stay and become line 5; the answers written there accumulate at the back of the book; recording goes until audio exists.
The Socruithe tab as a screen. Name, class, reminder time, strict fadas and clear go on the cover, reached by tapping the candidate box.
The questions-per-round setting (sessionSize). The page is five lines.
The stage picker in settings. Class number chooses the spine.
The Tosaigh button on the home screen and the home screen itself as a separate view. The app opens on tonight's page.
The streak ("lá as a chéile"), sessions today, due count, learned count and total on HomeView, and the "maith ✓" pen mark that repeats last night's score on the home page.
The running fraction and "Ceist n de N" in the ExamHeader, and the unit labels "Aonad 1 · Cuimhne", "Aonad 3 · Gramadach".
ResultsView as a separate screen, with "Babhta eile" as a primary button. The marked page is the result; another page is a small link.
The Leitner intervals 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 30; replaced by 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 with last night's wrong word forced to line 1.

GCSE as the default stage for a fresh install (Store defaults stage to .gcse and class to 11). Default to the class typed on the cover; for Years 8 to 10 that is the Key Stage 3 spine, which the proposal ruled the primary spine.

The 60 function words in the top 100 of the Key Stage 3 rank list (an, agus, ar, na, i, ag, le, go) as word-line prompts. "Write the Irish for 'the'" is a bad line; these words are met only inside line 4 and line 5, and word lines start from the nouns, verbs and adjectives in the list.
The system font as the print face; the mock-up's Atkinson Hyperlegible is bundled and registered the same way MarkingHand is.
risks: Coverage. Three word lines a night is roughly 50 to 60 distinct words a month retained, against a GCSE list of 2,233 entries and a Key Stage 3 list of 826. This app forms a habit and secures retention; it does not cover the list, and the department's classwork must. If "Leathanach eile?" is ever made prominent to chase coverage, the angle collapses.

Line 5 cannot be truly marked. There are no model answers, no teacher view and no Irish speech or grammar checker. The pen marks only what the rule engine can prove (a known word missing its fada, a known noun unlenited after a known preposition and article) and otherwise ticks the line as written. A pupil can author a wrong sentence on page 6 and rehearse it faithfully on page 20. A teacher view that surfaces the answer bank, or teacher-checked model answers for the 270 questions, is needed before this line is relied on for the speaking exam.

No audio. The nightly page has nothing spoken, so the speaking exam is rehearsed in writing only, and the Key Stage 3 phonics strand (the 62 sound-symbol correspondences) has no place on the page at all until the Abair Ulster voice is available. Recording without playback in a voice is not worth the screen.

The GCSE list carries 827 masculine marks and no feminine mark, plus 14 broken entries and sub-heading bleed. Until the cleaning workbook is done, line 4 must draw only on the 362 gender-tagged Key Stage 3 nouns, even for Year 11 and 12 pupils, and the GCSE word lines will occasionally show a faulty entry.

The marking hand font must carry á, é, í, ó, ú, the tick and the cross, and enough letters to write corrections like "fhuinneog" and "ar an bhord"; the digitised sample sheet needs checking against that set before corrections are written in it.

Marking a recalled answer against the pupil's own earlier sentence will be harsh on legitimate rephrasing. It should be lenient on function words and word order and strict only on content words and fadas, and that tolerance needs tuning with real pupils.

No streak and no counters is a hypothesis about motivation for this fork, not a proven one. Some pupils, including some with ADHD, respond to a chain. The page number is the compromise and should be tested with a small group before the design is fixed.
iOS may not reliably raise the keyboard on launch without a user tap; if not, the first tap on the live line is the start, which is still one action.

The relationship to Nathán is unknown beyond its being a word-scramble game. If Nathán holds pupil accounts or a class view, the copybook should share them rather than build its own; if it does not, a teacher view is new ground.
Copyright. The list inside a distributed app is a permissions question for the awarding body, already flagged in the proposal, and the app must never name that body or the curriculum documents.
A five-minute task on a phone at eight o'clock competes with everything else on that phone. The school iPad may be the better home for Years 8 to 10; that is a deployment decision, not a design one.

concepts.angle: The teacher's red pen at home. The app is not a course, a game or a dictionary: it is one copybook that the pupil writes a page in every school night and that a real teacher's pen (Dáithí's digitised hand, in St Paul's red) marks on the spot, correction beside the mistake, total and one-line comment at the foot. Every marked page is kept, in order, and the mistakes the pen has written twice come back on tomorrow's page. Nathán makes the pupil recognise a word; this makes them write it from memory and be marked. Everything the app has to say to the pupil, it says in the margin, in the hand, the way it would be said on a page handed back in class.
concepts.workingTitle: Suggestion only: "Peann Dearg" (the red pen; the thing the app is, and the colour pupils already know from marked work at St Paul's). Second choice: "Cóipleabhar" (copybook; the thing the pupil keeps). The current name "Cuimhne" (memory) names a faculty, not what the app does, and is one reason the point does not come through.
concepts.purpose: You write a page of Irish every night; a real teacher's red pen marks it straight away.
concepts.promise: After four weeks at five nights a week the pupil holds a copybook of about 20 dated, numbered, marked pages in their own biro blue, with every correction written beside its mistake in the teacher's hand. That is roughly 100 things written from memory: about 60 to 70 words from the list for their stage (frequency list in Years 8 to 10, topic list in Years 11 and 12), about 20 verbs with their verbal noun, about 15 article or preposition forms in Ulster shape (an tseachtain, ar an bhord), and 15 to 20 written answers of their own to the examiner's conversation questions, each marked for fadas, mutations and whether it carries an opinion and a reason. They also hold a single page at the back, "Mo chuid botún", listing the words and rules the pen has had to correct twice, and they can see with their own eyes that page 20 carries fewer red marks than page 1. None of that existed before: the pupil had a scramble score.
concepts.forWhom: Pupils of St Paul's, Bessbrook, aged 11 to 16, doing Irish as a subject: Years 8 to 10 on the frequency list of 826 words (the list that carries gender and part of speech), Years 11 and 12 on the topic list of 2,233 entries and the 270 examiner questions. First audience, by the principal's ruling: pupils with ADD and ADHD who cannot hold a long queue in their head and need to be marked now, not next week. Second audience: the Year 12 pupil building prepared personal answers for the speaking conversation. Not the teacher: there is no teacher view in this concept, only a page the pupil can show.

thread.idea: One copybook, marked every night. The whole app is a single copybook with a red margin that belongs to the pen. The pupil owns the lines; the pen owns the margin. The app has no features, only pages: tonight's page (blank, waiting), the pages already marked (kept, numbered, dated), and the back pages (the pupil's own answers, and the pen's list of what it has had to correct twice). The front cover carries the purpose in one line, in the hand, and it never goes away.
thread.onEveryScreen: Every screen is a page of the same copybook, so every screen has the same three fixed things: the candidate box at the top (Ainm, Rang, Dáta, Lch n, where n is the count of pages the pupil has filled, so the box itself is the progress), the pink margin rule at 44pt, and the pen's presence in that margin. Front page: the margin carries last night's closing note in the hand ("4/5, buail le arís amárach"), which is the reason tonight's page exists. Item page: the margin is empty until Seiceáil, then the tick or cross appears there and the correction appears over the answer line, and nothing else moves. Closed page: the pen's total and one-line comment sit at the foot, in the margin column. The copybook: every kept page opens exactly as it was marked, marks and all. Back pages: each written answer to an examiner question carries its own marks; the botún page is written entirely in the hand, because it is the pen's list, not the app's. Cúl an chóipleabhair (settings): the pupil's name and class in biro blue inside the candidate box, the stage written by the pen ("Bliain 9"). Red on any screen is the pen and only the pen; if something is red, the teacher wrote it. The purpose line at the top of every screen is in the paper's rubric italic and says what this page is for in the paper's own wording.
thread.whyNotGeneric: The marks are in one named teacher's real handwriting, in the red the pupils see on their own marked work at St Paul's, and they say what that teacher would say in the Ulster dialect the school teaches: "séimhiú, ní urú!", "fada!", "an tseachtain". A wrong article is not "incorrect", it is diagnosed by rule from the word's gender in the frequency list (Grammar.swift already does this for the article and nine prepositions). The questions are the 270 the examiner will actually ask, by topic, and the pupil's own answers to them accumulate as their prepared answers. The pages are kept the way a copybook is kept, not reset the way a game is. And it is the sister of Nathán: Nathán is the word seen, this is the word written and handed back.

firstRun.ga: Seo do chóipleabhar. Gach oíche scríobhann tú cúpla rud agus ceartaím é ar an bhomaite, leis an pheann dhearg. Ní scrúdú é. Rud ar bith atá contráilte, scríobhfaidh mé an leagan ceart sa chiumhais agus tiocfaidh sé ar ais chugat. Coinnigh achan leathanach. Scríobh d'ainm sa bhosca.
firstRun.en: This is your copybook. Each night you write a few things and I mark them straight away, in red pen. It is not a test. Anything wrong, I write the right version in the margin and it comes back until you have it. Write your name in the box.

home.headline: Leathanach an lae (today's page): the front of tonight's blank page, not a dashboard. Purpose line under the candidate box, in rubric italic: "Cúig rud le scríobh ó chuimhne. Ceartaím iad ar an bhomaite." with the grey English gloss "Five things to write from memory. I mark them straight away."
home.shows: Three things and nothing else. (1) The candidate box: Ainm and Rang in biro blue as the pupil wrote them, today's date, and "Lch 24": the page number is the only count on the screen, and it can only go up. (2) Last night's closing note in the margin, in the hand: "4/5, buail le arís amárach" or, on the first night, the front-cover line "Leathanach amháin achan oíche." This is the thread made visible: the pen's last word is the reason for tonight. (3) Tonight's rubric on the ruled lines, in the paper's wording: "Cúig rud: trí fhocal, an t-alt, ceist amháin", so the pupil knows the size and shape before they start; under it, the top edge of last night's marked page showing faintly, which is the way into the copybook. No streak, no "focal ar eolas as 3,059", no due count, no topic picker: those are the app talking about itself, and the principal's complaint was that nothing tells the pupil what it is for.
home.singleAction: One button below the paper, in print, not in the hand: "Scríobh" (Write). It opens item 1 of tonight's page with the keyboard up and the fada row showing. Nothing else on the front page is a button except the faint page edge.

structure.screen: Clúdach (front cover, first run only, then reachable from the back cover)
structure.purposeLine: Seo do chóipleabhar. Leathanach amháin achan oíche; ceartaím é.
structure.content: The first-run text above, written in the hand on ruled lines, with the English gloss in grey print beneath. An empty candidate box the pupil fills in biro blue (name, class) and a single question in the paper's rubric italic: "Cén bhliain ina bhfuil tú?" with Bliain 8 to 12 as five printed boxes to tick; this sets the stage (frequency list for 8 to 10, topic list for 11 and 12) without ever naming a curriculum or board. One button: "Oscail".

structure.screen: Leathanach an lae (today's page, the home)
structure.purposeLine: Cúig rud le scríobh ó chuimhne. Ceartaím iad ar an bhomaite.
structure.content: As described under home: candidate box with page number, last night's note in the margin in the hand, tonight's rubric naming the five things, faint edge of the last marked page, one button "Scríobh". Tonight's five are chosen by the scheduler: what is due from the Leitner boxes (shortened for the ADHD fork to 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 days), anything the pen corrected twice, then new items from the stage's list to fill the page. The mix is fixed in shape so every page looks like the last: three words (one of them a verb with its verbal noun where the list has one; 412 verbs, 358 with a verbal noun), one grammar item, one written answer to an examiner question.

structure.purposeLine: Scríobh an focal ceart sa bhosca. (Write the correct word in the box.)
structure.content: One item per screen. Item number in bold, the English prompt on the first rule ("to meet (someone)"), the answer box on the next rule in biro blue; for a verb, two boxes, "Fréamh + réamhfhocal" and "Ainm briathartha", as in ExamRecall.dc.html. Seiceáil marks on the spot: tick or cross in the margin in the hand, the right form written in red over a struck-through wrong answer, "fada!" over a form right but for the fada when strict fadas is off. Blank plus Seiceáil is allowed and is marked "?" with the answer written in: no separate "Taispeáin dom" reveal. A wrong item is put back onto this same page as item 6, headed "Arís". Ar aghaidh moves on; nothing else on the screen changes. Gender is not shown beside the prompt for KS3 nouns; if the pupil later gets the article wrong the pen writes "bain.!" and that is how gender is taught.

structure.purposeLine: Cuir le chéile. Scríobh an fhoirm cheart. (Put together. Write the correct form.)
structure.content: The same page layout, one item: "an + seachtain" or "ar an + bord" with the English in grey, one answer line. The rule engine in Grammar.swift produces the Ulster form and, on a wrong answer, the pen writes the diagnosis in the margin in its own words ("urú, ní séimhiú!", "séimhiú de dhíth", "t roimh s") and the one-line rule beneath the answer in the hand, with the English gloss in grey print; no bordered rule box in print. Drawn only from nouns that carry a gender, which today means the 362 KS3 nouns (116 feminine); the GCSE list marks 827 masculine and no feminine, so it cannot feed this item until cleaned. Later item kinds from the same data, in the same layout: the 29 prepositional pronouns in the KS3 list as a straight recall ("at me" gives "agam"), and possessives.

structure.purposeLine: Freagair an cheist. Dhá líne. (Answer the question. Two lines.)
structure.content: One of the 270 examiner questions, chosen from the topics the pupil's stage allows (Years 8 to 10 get the "Mé féin" questions such as Q001 "Cad é an t-ainm atá ort?" and the school ones; Years 11 and 12 the full 12 topics), printed on the first rule; two ruled lines to write on; a small round record button in the margin below the pen's space for the pupil to say it after writing it. The pen marks what it can honestly mark from the data: each word is looked up in the stage list, a word right but for the fada gets "fada!" over it; a noun after "ar an", "sa", "leis an" and the other seven is checked for Ulster lenition; the pen ticks in the margin if the answer contains one of the 27 opinion frames ("is maith liom", "is fearr liom", "tá dúil agam i") and a reason word ("mar", "mar gheall ar"); a word in neither list gets a faint grey "?" in print, never red, meaning "I do not know this word", and the pen writes nothing about it. If the answer is a sentence with nothing the pen can check, it writes "scríofa" and a tick, not a mark. The answer and the recording are kept as the pupil's own answer to that question, in the back pages.

structure.purposeLine: Ceartaithe. (Marked.)
structure.content: The whole page as it was written, all five (or six) items on the rules with their marks in the margin, the date and page number in the candidate box, the pen's total "4/5" and one comment in the hand at the foot: "maith thú", "buail le arís amárach", "an fada, a Aoife". Only now is the pupil offered more: "Leathanach eile?" as a link, and "Dún" as the button, which files the page and returns to the front, where the margin note now shows tonight's comment. This is the screen the pupil can show a parent or teacher: a share sheet exports it as an image of the page, marks and all.

structure.purposeLine: Do chuid leathanach, mar a ceartaíodh iad. (Your pages, as they were marked.)
structure.content: Reached by the faint page edge on the front. A vertical run of kept pages, newest at the bottom, each shown as a page with its number and date and its marks, never as a list row with a score. Tap a page to open it as it was. Tap any red correction on any page and the link "Cuir ar leathanach an lae amárach" puts that item on tomorrow's page: the pupil chooses their own revision from their own mistakes. Nights not done are not shown: page numbers run 23, 24, 25 whatever the dates, so a missed week is not a row of gaps. Ends with two back pages, below.

structure.screen: Cúl 1: Mo chuid freagraí (my answers, a back page)
structure.purposeLine: Do chuid freagraí féin ar cheisteanna an chomhrá. (Your own answers to the conversation questions.)
structure.content: The 270 questions grouped under their 12 topics in the paper's wording, each row the question and, if the pupil has answered it, their answer in biro blue with the pen's marks and a play button for the recording. Unanswered questions have an empty ruled line. "Ceist eile ón ábhar seo" puts one more question from that topic onto tonight's page. This is the personal answer bank the speaking exam rewards, built one page at a time rather than as a separate module.

structure.screen: Cúl 2: Mo chuid botún (my mistakes, a back page)
structure.purposeLine: Na rudaí a cheartaigh mé faoi dhó. (The things I have corrected twice.)
structure.content: Written entirely in the hand: the words and forms the pen has corrected on two or more pages, grouped under the pen's own headings ("fada", "séimhiú", "urú, ní séimhiú", "ainm briathartha", "focail"), each with the right form and the page numbers where it went wrong, so the pupil can turn back to them. A word leaves this page when it has been right on three pages running, and the pen crosses it out rather than deleting it. This page is what "regular recall" looks like from the pupil's side.

structure.screen: Cúl an chóipleabhair (the back cover; settings)
structure.purposeLine: Do chuid sonraí. (Your details.)
structure.content: Still a page, not a system form: the candidate box, editable (name, class), the year ticked as on the front cover, "Fadaí dochta" as a tick box in the rubric wording, "Am an leathanaigh" for one optional daily reminder at a time the pupil picks, and "Glan an cóipleabhar" as the only destructive act, with confirmation. A last line in grey print: whose hand the marking is in.

concepts.dailyLoop: 1. About 8pm, the reminder \"Do leathanach\" or the pupil opens the app. Front page: candidate box reads Lch 24, the margin carries last night's note \"4/5, buail le arís amárach\", and the rubric says tonight is \"Cúig rud: trí fhocal, an t-alt, ceist amháin\". Tap \"Scríobh\". (15 seconds.) 2. Item 1, headed \"Arís\": \"to meet (someone)\". Types \"buail le\" and \"ag bualadh\" (last night it was \"ag buala\"). Seiceáil: two ticks in the margin. Ar aghaidh. (30 seconds.) 3. Item 2: \"at me\" (a KS3 prepositional pronoun, rank 100). Types \"agam\". Tick. (15 seconds.) 4. Item 3: \"an + seachtain\". Types \"an seachtain\". Cross; the pen writes \"an tseachtain\" over the struck-through answer and \"bain.! t roimh s\" in the margin, and the rule under it in the hand with the English gloss in grey. Ar aghaidh. (30 seconds.) 5. Item 4: \"however\" from tonight's topic. Types \"afach\". Margin tick with \"fada! áfach\" over it, because strict fadas is off in Year 9. (20 seconds.) 6. Item 5: Q182 \"Cad é an t-ábhar is fearr leat?\" on the first rule, two lines to write. Types \"Is maith liom Gaeilge mar ta se suimiuil.\" Seiceáil: \"fada!\" over \"ta se suimiuil\" with the three right forms above, a tick in the margin for opinion and reason. Taps record, says it, stops. (75 seconds.) 7. Item 6, \"Arís\": \"an + seachtain\" again. Types \"an tseachtain\". Tick. (15 seconds.) 8. The page closes: all six items on the rules with their marks, \"5/6\" and \"na fadaí, a Aoife\" in the hand at the foot, date and Lch 24 in the box. \"Dún\". Front page now shows tonight's note. Total about four minutes; \"Leathanach eile?\" was offered once, at the close, and ignored.
concepts.register: Keep it, because under this angle the exam-script register is not decoration, it is the product: a marked page is the only thing the app makes, and ruled lines, a red margin, a candidate box and a pen hand are what a marked page looks like. But it must be made to serve, which the proof of concept does not do, and that means rules on every screen. (1) Red is the pen and nothing else: no red borders, no red boxes, no red buttons; the pink margin rule stays pink. If it is red, the teacher wrote it. (2) The pen only writes what a teacher writes on a page: a tick, a cross, a \"?\", the correct form, a note of two to six words, a total, a one-line comment, a rule in one line. Never a heading, a label, a count, a button or a sentence of instruction. The hand font has one form per letter and no kerning, so anything longer than a line looks typed and breaks the spell. (3) The candidate box is the same on every screen and carries name, class, date and page number; never a score, never a percentage, never \"11/11\" while a page is in progress. Marks live in the margin per item and at the foot of the closed page. (4) The rubric italic with grey English gloss is the purpose line of every screen and uses the papers' own wording (\"Scríobh an focal ceart sa bhosca\", \"Cuir le chéile\", \"Freagair an cheist\"). (5) The ruled paper is the writing area only; the print buttons sit below it and there are at most two: one filled (Seiceáil, Ar aghaidh, Dún) and one link. (6) Typed answers sit on the rule in biro blue at the same line height as the rules, so the page reads as written on, not as fields over a background. (7) Things that defeat the register go: the five-tab bar (a copybook has no tabs), the system-styled Settings Form, the streak and word counts on the front page, the print rule box with the red border in Grammar.swift, and the \"Sampla:\" line in ExamRecall.dc.html, which quotes example sentences that do not exist in the data. (8) The register must not become the exam: no timer, no tier, no \"Foundation/Higher\", and the pen's language stays kind (\"arís amárach\", never \"wrong\").
concepts.adhd: The concept is built for this fork first, not adapted to it. One item per screen, one answer line, one button. A page is always five things and the pupil is told the five before starting; the queue behind them (what is due, how many words in the list) is never shown. Marking is immediate on Seiceáil and physical: the tick lands in the margin where the pupil is looking, the correction lands on the wrong word, and nothing else on the screen moves. An item wrong tonight comes back on the same page within two minutes, so the pupil sees themselves get it right before the page closes, which is the in-session progress the ruling asked for. The intervals are shorter than the proof of concept's (0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 days rather than 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 30) and anything corrected twice is put on the next page regardless of interval. Every page has the same shape (three words, one grammar item, one answer) and every item screen the same layout, so there is nothing to work out. The page number is the only count, and it only goes up; a missed week leaves no gaps in the copybook and the pen never mentions it. Sound is off, there is no timer, no percentage, no red on screen except the pen's own marks, and \"Leathanach eile?\" is offered once, after the page is closed, never before. The reminder is one, at a time the pupil chose, and it says \"Do leathanach\", not \"You have 37 words due\". The pen's comments are short enough to be read in one glance, and their register is the kind teacher's, because a pupil who has just seen five crosses needs \"arís amárach, a Aoife\", not a score.
cuts: The five-tab bar (Inniu, Innéacs, Gramadach, Labhairt, Socruithe) in CuimhneApp.swift: a copybook has no tabs, and the tabs are what makes it read as an app with features rather than a thing with a purpose.
Innéacs (IndexView.swift): browsing 39 groups with learned counts is a dictionary page, which the principal rejected; topic scope comes in through the scheduler and the answer bank instead.

The front-page lines "focal le déanamh inniu", "focal ar eolas, as 3059", "lá as a chéile" and "babhta déanta inniu" in HomeView.swift: the app talking about itself in print; replaced by the pen's last note and tonight's rubric.
The running score in the candidate box during a page ("11/11" in ExamRecall.dc.html, scoreText in SessionView.swift): marks belong in the margin per item and at the foot of the closed page.
Gramadach as an endless standalone drill ("Ceist eile" loop with no page, no end, no record) in Grammar.swift: it becomes one item on every page.
Labhairt as a three-level navigation (topic list, question list, question) in SpeakingView.swift: replaced by one written-answer item per page plus the back page "Mo chuid freagraí".
The "Taispeáin dom" reveal link: a blank answer is marked "?" and the pen writes the answer in, which is what happens on a real page.
The gender label "(fir.)" / "(bain.)" shown beside the English prompt before marking: it gives away what the article item is testing; the pen writes "bain.!" when it matters.
The print rule box with the red border and white background in Grammar.swift: the rule is one line in the hand with a grey gloss, and red is reserved for the pen.
The "Sampla: Buailim le mo chairde gach Satharn." line in the ExamRecall mock-up: there are no example sentences in the data and none should be invented for the screen.
The system Form in SettingsView.swift with grouped grey rows: replaced by the back cover, drawn as a page.

The ResultsView comment set ("maith thú!", "arís amárach", "n le foghlaim") as fixed strings: the closing comment should name the item or the fault ("buail le arís amárach", "na fadaí"), otherwise the hand says nothing a teacher would say.
Leitner intervals 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 30 in Models.swift: shortened for the first audience and overridden by the twice-corrected rule.
The name Cuimhne, if the principal agrees: it is a feature name and it appears in the header of every screen as "Aonad 1 · Cuimhne", which reads as a unit of a course.
risks: Marking free writing is the biggest promise and the thinnest capability. With no model answers and no parser, the pen can only check each word against the stage list (fada-insensitive), check Ulster lenition after the nine prepositions and the article, and look for one of the 27 opinion frames and a reason word. That is spell-check-grade marking dressed in a teacher's hand. The concept handles it by having the pen mark only what it knows, put a grey print "?" on unknown words rather than a red cross, and write "scríofa" when it has nothing to say; but a pupil may still read silence as approval. Model answers (about 270 questions at two levels, Ulster Irish, signed off by an Irish teacher) or a teacher's pass over the answers are needed before the pen can honestly mark a sentence.

No audio. Apple ships no Irish voice or recogniser, so the written-answer item shows the question in print and the pupil's recording is record-and-listen only, unmarked. The Abair Ulster voice (Trinity College Dublin) is needed to read the 270 questions aloud, to make a cold-conversation mode, and for any phonics item over the 62 sound-symbol correspondences, which this concept leaves out of the first build for that reason.

The hand font is a first cut: one form per letter, no kerning, no apostrophe, no double quote, no semicolon, so "d'ainm" and "b'fhéidir" cannot be written in the hand today, and anything longer than a few words looks mechanical and gives the conceit away. It needs at least a second form of the common letters, an apostrophe, and a limit in code on the length of any pen note.

The GCSE list carries 827 masculine nouns and no feminine (feminine was marked only by absence in the source), so the article and preposition items cannot be drawn from it until the cleaning workbook is finished; until then those items come only from the 362 KS3 nouns, and a Year 11 pupil gets grammar items from the wrong list. The prep field in vocab.json is populated for only 7 verbs (6 le, 1 ar), so "the governing preposition" is largely unstructured. The group "Nathanna coitianta" contains 29 rows of summary statistics from the KS3 workbook ("Total entries 800", "n = masculine noun 236") that would appear as prompts; and "dúinn" appears twice.

Red pen carries baggage. A pupil who gets 0/5 sees five crosses in the school's marking colour on their first night. The kind register of the comments and the shortened intervals are the mitigation on paper; it needs trying with three or four pupils from the target group before it is trusted, and the closing comment wording needs an Irish teacher's ear.

No teacher view. The copybook is private to the device; the only bridge to the department is the pupil exporting a page as an image. A class view, or a nightly export beside the rest of Cumarsáid, is a later build, and until then the app is a private habit rather than a department tool.

Pages are kept forever on one device with no iCloud sync in this concept; a lost or replaced phone loses the copybook, which under this angle is the whole point of four weeks' work. Sync should come before any wide roll-out.

Copyright: every kept page reproduces entries from the examining body's list, and the app never names the source. Internal school use is ordinary practice; the App Store is a permissions question that stands unchanged.

The concept assumes the pupil types Irish on an iPhone keyboard with the fada row; long-press accents are slow for this audience, so the fada row must be in place on every item screen, including the two-line answer, or the page takes eight minutes rather than four.
All Irish copy in this concept, including the first-run text, the rubric lines and the pen's stock phrases, needs sign-off by a named Irish teacher for Ulster form before it is shown to a pupil.

concepts.angle: The road from Year 8 to Year 12, made visible. The data already falls into nine stops in a fixed order: six frequency bands from the Key Stage 3 list (76, 95, 117, 177, 236 and 96 headwords: the 100 commonest, 101 to 250, 251 to 500, 501 to 1000, 1001 to 2000, beyond 2000) and then the three GCSE contexts (Mé féin, mo shaol agus mo chultúr, 811 words and 86 examiner questions; Mo cheantar, an tír agus an domhan, 685 words and 93 questions; Saol na scoile agus saol na hoibre, 320 words and 91 questions), with the 417 general words (numbers, days, prepositions, opinions, connectives) threaded through the GCSE stops. The 62 sound-symbol correspondences sit at the first stop, because their source words (an, is, mo, rud, tá, mé, sí, tú, maith, bia, fuair) are themselves in the first band. The 48-point grammar checklist is broken into short pages that use each stop's own nouns and verbs. The product is not the drill; it is that the pupil can always see what is behind them, where they are, and what is next, and that every five-minute session moves a number they can point to. In the exam-script register the road already has a native form: the marks grid on the front cover of an answer booklet, one row per question, filled in red by the marker. Here the grid has nine rows, one per stop, and it is filled in over five years.
concepts.workingTitle: Suggestion only: "Bealach" (the way, the road; Ulster usage as in "ar an bhealach", on the way). The current name Cuimhne (memory) describes one task; Bealach describes the whole.
concepts.purpose: Every Irish word and speaking question from Year 8 to GCSE, in order, with the ones you know ticked off.
concepts.promise: A Year 8 pupil doing five words a night, four nights a week, has seen about 80 words; with the Leitner rule (a word is "known" after two right answers a day or more apart) roughly 60 to 70 are ticked, so Céim 1 (the 76 commonest words) is signed off and dated in red on the cover and Céim 2 has started, and the ten vowel sounds have been read aloud and recorded. A Year 11 pupil has about 60 words of one topic ticked, two six-question grammar pages marked, and four written answers to real examiner questions kept in their own book. In both cases the cover shows it: one row signed, one row with a number that grew every night, seven rows still to come. The pupil can hand the phone to a parent or teacher and say "I am at Céim 2".
concepts.forWhom: Pupils of St Paul's aged 11 to 16 learning Irish, from a Year 8 who starts at Céim 1 to a Year 12 who starts at Céim 9 with two years of GCSE words and questions in front of them. Built first for the pupil with ADD or ADHD who needs to be told, on every screen, where they are and what the one next thing is. Not for teachers yet: there is no teacher view, and the marks are the app's, not a person's.

thread.idea: The app is one answer booklet that takes five years to fill. Its front cover is the road: the candidate box, then the marker's grid with nine numbered rows, Céim 1 to Céim 9, each a real band or context from the two lists. A row is blank until the pupil reaches it, carries a running count in red while they are on it (41 as 117), and is ticked and dated in the marking hand when its words are known, its grammar page marked and, for GCSE stops, its questions answered. Every page inside the booklet belongs to one row, and is numbered the way exam questions are numbered: 3.1 is the words of Céim 3, 3.2 its grammar page, 3.3 its questions, 1.0 the sounds.
thread.onEveryScreen: The candidate box on every page has four cells. Top: Ainm and Rang in biro. Bottom left: the stop, always, in the same wording as the cover row (Céim 3 · Focail 251 go 500). Bottom right: the page number and position (3.1 · Ceist 2 de 5) with the mark so far in red. The rubric line under the box is the page's purpose line, in the papers' own wording where one exists. The margin holds marks only. Every marked page ends with one line in the marking hand that reports the road moving: Céim 3: 41 → 44 as 117. Back from any page goes to the cover, never to a list of tabs. The results page, the grammar page and the speaking page all close with that same red road line, so a pupil never finishes a task without seeing where it put them.
thread.whyNotGeneric: The nine rows are the school's own two lists in the order the framework and the exam impose, not levels invented for a game: the row names are the band names and the context names from the data (Na 100 focal is coitianta, Mo cheantar, an tír agus an domhan). The 270 questions, the Ulster forms in the grammar engine and the sign-off in the principal's own hand cannot be transplanted to French. There is no experience bar, no ring, no streak, no leaderboard: progress is a count in a marker's grid and a dated tick, which is what progress looks like on marked work at St Paul's.

firstRun.ga: Seo an bealach ó Bhliain 8 go GCSE: achan fhocal agus achan cheist a bheas de dhíth ort, in ord. Cúig fhocal in aghaidh na hoíche, agus cuirfidh mise tic leo sa chiumhais. Ní scrúdú é seo ach do chóipleabhar féin. Tosaímis ag Céim 1: na 100 focal is coitianta.
firstRun.en: This is the road from Year 8 to GCSE: every word and every question you will need, in order. Five words a night, and I tick them in the margin. It is not a test, it is your own copybook. We start at Step 1: the 100 commonest words.

home.headline: An bealach ó Bhliain 8 go GCSE. Tá tú ag Céim 3: Focail 251 go 500.
home.shows: Three things and nothing else. First, the cover grid: nine ruled rows, Céim 1 to Céim 9, each with its band or context name and its word count (and, for rows 7 to 9, its question count). Rows behind the pupil carry a tick and a date in the marking hand; the current row carries the live count in red (41 as 117) and the word anseo in the margin; rows ahead are in ink with no mark. This answers where am I. Second, one line under the grid for tonight: Anocht: 5 fhocal (3 le hathdhéanamh, 2 nua), built from what is due in the current stop, and, once a stop's words are mostly in box 1 or above, a second line: Anocht fosta: Gramadach 3.2, 6 cheist. This answers what do I do. Third, last night's mark in the box's right cell in red (aréir 4/5). This answers how did I do. No streak, no learned total across the whole list, no sessions-today count: those are the numbers that were on the PoC home page and none of them tells a pupil where they are on a road.
