home.singleAction: Tosaigh: starts tonight's five words from the current stop. Tapping a row of the grid opens that stop's page; nothing else on the cover is tappable.

structure.purposeLine: An bealach ó Bhliain 8 go GCSE. Tá tú ag Céim 3.
structure.content: Candidate box (Ainm, Rang, Bliain). The marker's grid: nine rows, band or context name, count, tick and date in red where signed off, anseo in the margin at the current row. Tonight's line. Tosaigh. The first-run words appear once, on the ruled lines below the grid, and are replaced by the tonight line thereafter.

structure.screen: Céim (one stop's page, reached by tapping its row)
structure.purposeLine: Céim 3 · Focail 251 go 500 · 41 as 117 ar eolas.
structure.content: The stop's pages listed as numbered questions on ruled lines: 3.1 Focail (117, with the count known and a Cleachtadh button), 3.2 Gramadach (an t-alt agus na réamhfhocail, 6 cheist, marked or not), and for GCSE stops 3.3 Ceisteanna (36 questions, 4 answered). Céim 1 alone has 1.0 Fuaimeanna (62). A link Féach ar an liosta opens the word list with ticks, but the list is behind a link, not on the page. What signs the row off is stated in one line at the foot: Tic ar an chlúdach nuair a bheas na focail ar eolas agus an ghramadach déanta.

structure.purposeLine: Scríobh an focal ceart sa bhosca. Write the correct word in the box.
structure.content: One word per screen, as in the PoC: English prompt with gender for nouns, one answer box (two for verbs: root plus preposition, and verbal noun), fada row, Seiceáil, tick or the right form written in red over the struck answer, fada! note when only the fada is wrong. Box cell reads Céim 3 · Focail 251 go 500 and 3.1 · Ceist 2 de 5 · 1/1. A word wrong first time returns at the end of the same five. Words come from the current stop only: due first, then new, never from the whole list.

structure.screen: Marcáil (results, the end of every task)
structure.purposeLine: Ceartaithe. Marked.
structure.content: The five words on ruled lines with ticks and crosses down the margin, the mark in the box (4/5), the marker's comment in red (maith thú, or 1 le foghlaim), and beneath it the road line in red: Céim 3: 41 → 44 as 117. When a stop is completed the line reads Céim 3 déanta, with the date, and the cover row is ticked when the pupil goes back. Two actions: Babhta eile, Clúdach.

structure.purposeLine: Cuir le chéile. Scríobh an fhoirm cheart. Put together. Write the correct form.
structure.content: Six questions, not an endless drill, generated from this stop's own nouns and verbs: article with a noun, preposition with the article in Ulster forms, possessives, and for GCSE stops verb forms in positive, negative and question. Wrong answers diagnosed by rule in the marking hand (urú, ní séimhiú!) with the rule in Irish and English on request. Ends with the road line. Six right first time marks the page done for that stop; the stop's later grammar pages (there is one per checklist area the stop supports) are numbered 3.2, 3.4 and so on.

structure.screen: Ceisteanna (a GCSE stop's speaking page, n.3)
structure.purposeLine: Freagair an cheist i nGaeilge. Labhair ar feadh 30 soicind ar a laghad. Answer in Irish. Speak for at least 30 seconds.
structure.content: One examiner question per screen from the stop's context (86, 93 or 91 questions), the pupil's own written answer on the ruled lines in biro, record and play back, the answer kept in the book. Marked only as answered or not (a tick in the margin when an answer is saved), because there is no model answer and no recognition. The stop's question count on the cover row moves. A Scrúdú fuar switch on this page alone picks questions at random from the stop with a countdown; it is off by default.

structure.purposeLine: Léigh os ard agus taifead. Read aloud and record.
structure.content: One sound per screen from the 62: the symbol, the source word from the frequency list, the cluster words, English gloss. The pupil reads aloud and records; playback; a tick in the margin when recorded. Hearing the sound first needs the Ulster voice, so until audio exists this page is read-and-record with no marking, and the cover counts it as done when all 62 are recorded.

structure.screen: Mo chuid focal (personal vocabulary, an extra page in every stop)
structure.purposeLine: Do chuid focal féin: do bhaile, do shloinne, do chlub.
structure.content: The framework's small personal vocabulary, which the appendix leaves placeholders for (a placename, the pupil's surname). The pupil adds a word and its English; it joins the current stop's five in rotation and carries the same tick. Kept to a short list; it is the pupil's own last lines on each stop's page, not a dictionary.

structure.purposeLine: Cé thú féin agus cá bhfuil tú ar an bhealach.
structure.content: Ainm, Rang, Bliain (which sets the starting stop: Year 8 to Céim 1, Year 11 to Céim 7; a pupil may move the anseo marker themselves), words per round (5, 10, 15), strict fadas, iCloud sync on or off, clear progress. No stage picker: Key Stage 3 and GCSE are one road.

concepts.dailyLoop: 1. Open the app. The cover appears with anseo beside Céim 3, the live count 41 as 117, and the line Anocht: 5 fhocal (3 le hathdhéanamh, 2 nua). About five seconds to read. 2. Tap Tosaigh. 3. Five words, one per screen: read the English, type the Irish with the fada row, tap Seiceáil, see the tick or the right form in red, tap Ar aghaidh. A word got wrong comes back as a sixth or seventh screen. About two to three minutes. 4. The marked page: ticks in the margin, 4/5 in red, one comment, and the road line Céim 3: 41 → 44 as 117. 5. Tap Clúdach: the cover row now shows 44 as 117. Done, in under five minutes. 6. If the pupil has more in them, Babhta eile runs another five; on nights when the cover shows Anocht fosta: Gramadach 3.2, the second round is the six-question grammar page instead, and on a GCSE stop one examiner question. The order never changes: cover, five words, mark, cover.
concepts.register: Keep it, with one addition that fixes the fault the principal saw. The canvas note on the exam-script row admitted that the register only made sense inside a task and left the home page in the dictionary register; the PoC then made the home page a task-shaped sheet of statistics, so nothing said what the app was for. The answer booklet already has a page that is not a task: its front cover, where the marker's grid lists every question and the marks go in red as they are earned. That grid, with nine rows for the nine stops, is the home screen and the statement of purpose, in the register's own furniture. On every screen the register must then do four jobs. The candidate box names the stop in its bottom-left cell and the page number and position in its bottom-right cell, so the pupil is never on a page without knowing which row of the cover it belongs to. The rubric line under the box is the purpose line, and where the papers have wording for the task (Scríobh an focal ceart sa bhosca; Freagair an cheist i nGaeilge) that wording is used. The margin carries marks only, in the digitised hand, in red: ticks, crosses, the right form, the diagnosis, the road line, the date on a signed-off row. Biro blue is the pupil's and nothing else is coloured. Nothing is decorative: a ruled line with no writing on it, a mark with no answer beside it, or a header cell that names an Aonad meaning nothing to a pupil is to be removed. Ticks and counts, no percentages; the only timer is the Scrúdú fuar switch the pupil turns on.
concepts.adhd: The road is the ADHD design, not an addition to it. A pupil who cannot hold a plan in their head is handed one: the cover says where they are and the tonight line says the one thing to do, and both are the same every night. Sessions are five words, from one stop, with the wrong ones re-tested inside the same round; no queue is ever shown up front, and the stop's full list is behind a link. Feedback is on the same screen within a second of Seiceáil, in a hand they know, and the road line at the end of every task is progress they can see in minutes (41 → 44), not days. Every task page has the same skeleton: box, rubric, ruled page, one answer, one button. The sign-off on the cover is a tick and a date, earned, with no streak to lose and no timer unless switched on. The Leitner intervals stay short (0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 30 days) and a stop stays live on the cover until it is signed, so returning after a bad week costs nothing but the due count.
cuts: The five-tab bar (Inniu, Innéacs, Gramadach, Labhairt, Socruithe) and the idea of five peer screens. Navigation is cover, stop, page, and back to the cover.
The home page as a sheet of statistics: learned total across the whole list, streak, sessions today, the Céad lá line. The cover grid replaces all of it; the streak goes entirely.
Sessions that draw on every topic of the current stage (Gach topaic). Five words come from the current stop only.
The Gramadach tab as an endless random drill with a running score. It becomes a six-question page belonging to a stop and using that stop's nouns.
The Innéacs as a separate browse-everything list. The word list lives behind a link on each stop's page.
The Labhairt topic index as a separate structure. The 270 questions live on the GCSE stops, grouped by the three contexts the data already carries.

The Stage picker (Eochairchéim 3 or GCSE) in settings and separate progress per stage. One road, one progress record; a headword known at a Key Stage 3 stop keeps its tick when it reappears in a GCSE stop (296 headwords are on both lists).
The Aonad 1, 2, 3 labels in the candidate box, which mean nothing to a pupil; the cell names the stop.
The 29 rows in the Key Stage 3 group Nathanna coitianta that are workbook totals (Total entries: 800, adj = adjective), which are in vocab.json as if they were words.
The Socruithe footer copy in English explaining the two lists; the road explains itself.
risks: The year-to-stop mapping (Year 8 at Céim 1, Year 11 at Céim 7) is an assumption. The Irish department's schemes of work decide the order; if they teach topics in Year 9, the road must be re-cut before it is shown to pupils.

Céim 1 is hard to drill by English-to-Irish typing: the 100 commonest words are largely function words (an, agus, ar, na, i, ag, le, go, is, mo). Recall from an English prompt for 'the' is meaningless. The stop needs a different task (a word in a short phrase, or the sound page) and there are no sentences or phrases in the data beyond the 17 multi-word items and 29 common phrases.

The Key Stage 3 list has 29 junk rows and 29 rows without part of speech, and one rank of 79410; the GCSE list is uncleaned (feminine gender largely unmarked: 116 f against 1,073 m across the file, 14 broken entries), so grammar pages at stops 7 to 9 would mark feminine nouns wrongly until the cleaning workbook replaces the JSON.
Sounds need audio to be phonics. Without the Ulster voice from Abair the 1.0 page is read-and-record with no marking, which the framework would not count as hearing the sound.

Speaking has no model answers and no recognition, so a question is only ever 'answered', never marked. A pupil may prepare a wrong answer for two years. Teacher feedback would need a teacher view, which does not exist.

The marks are in the principal's hand but are the app's marks. A pupil or parent could take a dated sign-off as a teacher's real assessment. The first-run words say mise; the settings page should say plainly that the marking is automatic.
The road spans five years, so progress must survive a change of phone. The PoC stores everything in UserDefaults on one device; iCloud sync is required before any pupil starts Year 8 on it.

Arithmetic: 2,233 GCSE words at five a night is 446 nights, more than two years of school nights. Either the GCSE stops allow ten to fifteen a night by default or the cover will honestly show a row that cannot be finished. The general words (417) also need a home on the road; threading them through stops 7 to 9 is a design decision not yet tested.

A pupil who joins in Year 11 sees six unsigned Key Stage 3 rows above them. Whether those rows read as 'behind you' or 'failed' needs a decision: a grey roimh an aip mark, or a quick placement check, neither of which exists.

The grammar engine covers the article and nine prepositions. The checklist has 48 points (39 Foundation, 9 Higher); possessives, verb forms in three shapes, counting objects and prepositional pronouns (29 in the KS3 list) are not yet generated, so stops 2 to 9 cannot yet have their grammar pages.
Copyright: the lists inside an App Store build are a permissions question already noted in the proposal; the road makes the lists the whole product.
The tick-and-date sign-off needs the marking font to carry digits and a slash; the digitised sample sheet must include them.

concepts.angle: The pupil's own Irish voice. The app is not a course and not a drill bank; it is one pupil's copybook of answers about their own life (name, townland, family, club, school, job, plans), written in their own words on ruled lines, spoken into the phone in their own voice, and marked in the margin in red. Every word drilled, every grammar item set and every conversation rehearsed comes out of a sentence the pupil wrote. The 270 examiner questions are the table of contents of that copybook: 12 topics become 12 chapters of "mo scéal", and the GCSE speaking exam is the day the pupil reads it aloud from memory. The Key Stage 3 framework's "small personal vocabulary", "writing from memory" and "unprepared speech" are the same thing at a younger age, so Years 8 to 10 use the same copybook with the 21 "Mé féin" questions and the yes/no questions (79 of the 270 start An, Ar or Nach) as their chapters.
concepts.workingTitle: Suggestion only: "Mo Ghlór" (my voice). Alternative if the principal wants the object rather than the idea: "Cóipleabhar" (copybook). The current name Cuimhne (memory) describes the mechanism, not the point.
concepts.purpose: Build your own answers in Irish about your life, so you can talk about yourself without notes.
concepts.promise: After four weeks of one question a night (about 25 school nights), the pupil has: 20 to 25 of their own answers written and recorded, covering the whole of "Mé féin, mo theaghlach" (21 questions) and the start of "Mo cheantar" (36 questions); a personal word list of roughly 80 to 120 words that came out of those answers and have been recalled from English at least three times over spaced intervals; the mutated forms of their own nouns (their townland after "i", their club after "ar an", their brother or sister after "mo") drilled until right; and the ability to answer any of those 20 to 25 questions aloud, in a cold run with the page hidden, for 20 to 40 seconds each. That is two to three minutes of unscripted talk about themselves, which they did not have before. It is also a booklet: the pupil can export the copybook as a PDF exam script and hand it to their Irish teacher.
concepts.forWhom: Pupils at St Paul's, Years 8 to 12, learning Ulster Irish. Two entry points on the same copybook: Years 8 to 10 answer the simple personal questions (Q001 to Q021 and the yes/no set) with the Key Stage 3 frequency list (826 headwords, 349 nouns with gender) as the suggestion bank; Years 11 and 12 work through all 12 topics with the GCSE topic list (2,233 entries) as the suggestion bank. First among these, the pupil with ADD or ADHD who cannot hold a list of 2,000 words in mind but can hold one question about their own dog, their own club, their own bedroom, and gets a red tick on it within a second of writing it.

thread.idea: One copybook, the pupil's own, filled page by page in answer to the questions an examiner will actually ask. Nothing appears in the app that did not come from a page the pupil wrote. The examiner's questions are the chapter headings of the pupil's own story ("Mo scéal"); the pupil's answers are the pages; the words in those answers are the vocabulary; the nouns in those answers are the grammar; the recordings of those answers are the speaking practice; the red pen in the margin is the only voice other than the pupil's.
thread.onEveryScreen: Three fixed devices on every page. First, the candidate box (kept from the exam-script register) gains a third row that is the same on every screen: left cell "Mo scéal · Mo cheantar · lch 3" (which chapter of the pupil's story this page belongs to and which page of the copybook it is), right cell "96 focal liom féin" (the running count of the pupil's own words, in biro blue in the pupil's box, never in red). The count rises on every screen, so the pupil sees the portfolio growing whether they are answering, recalling, or doing grammar. Second, a provenance line in grey under every item on every drill screen: a recalled word shows "ó: Cá bhfuil tú i do chónaí?" and the pupil's own sentence containing it; a grammar item shows "ó: Déan cur síos ar do sheomra leapa" and the phrase they wrote; a cold-exam question shows "d'fhreagair tú é seo Dé Máirt". The pupil is never asked about a word they did not use. Third, ruled lines carry only the pupil's own writing in biro blue. No screen shows ruled lines with printed statistics on them (the current home does this and it is why the register reads as decoration). If there is nothing of the pupil's to put on the lines, the lines are not drawn.
thread.whyNotGeneric: A generic language app drills a fixed list downwards from the top; this one has no content until the pupil writes some. Its question bank is the 270 questions a teacher-examiner at this school draws from, in Ulster Irish (cad é, cad chuige, fosta), tagged to the three Contexts for Learning that also tag the vocabulary, so the suggestion bank under each answer is drawn from the matching Context. Its grammar engine mutates the pupil's own townland and club in Ulster forms (ar an bhord, sa charr, leis an mhúinteoir), which no store app does. Its marker is the principal's own hand in the school's red. And its end product is a booklet the pupil made, not a score.

firstRun.ga: Seo do chóipleabhar féin. Tá ceisteanna ann fút féin: cé thú féin, cá bhfuil tú i do chónaí, cad é a dhéanann tú. Freagair ceist amháin anois, i nGaeilge, i do chuid focal féin. Cuirfidh an peann dearg nóta sa chiumhais. Lá i ndiaidh lae, líonfaidh tú é.
firstRun.en: This is your own copybook. The questions in it are all about you: who you are, where you live, what you do. Answer one question now, in Irish, in your own words. The red pen will leave a note in the margin. Day by day, you will fill it.

home.headline: Mo scéal (the pupil's story), with the pupil's own name in the candidate box above it and today's single question printed in full on the page, waiting for an answer.
home.shows: Three things and no more. (1) Today's question, printed large in the examiner box exactly as the bank words it, for example Q002 "Cá bhfuil tú i do chónaí?", with its chapter name above it ("Mo cheantar"). It is the next unanswered question in the current chapter, so the pupil never chooses from a list. (2) Yesterday's page, reduced: the first line of the pupil's last answer in biro blue on one ruled line, with the pen's margin note from it still there ("fada? Bhéal Átha an Airgid ✓"). This is the evidence that the copybook is theirs and is filling. (3) The running count in the candidate box: "14 fhreagra · 96 focal liom féin". Not shown: streak, due counts, learned-out-of-2,233, last score, any percentage. Those are the app's numbers, not the pupil's story, and the principal's condition 2 (practice booklet, not a test) rules them out of the front page.
home.singleAction: Freagair (Answer). One dark button. If the pupil has three or more of their own words due for recall, a second, smaller line under it reads "3 fhocal le cuimhneamh ar dtús" and the tap goes through that 60-second recall first, then to the question. There is no other action on the home page; chapters, playback and export are reached from the candidate box (tap the "Mo scéal" cell).

structure.purposeLine: Do chóipleabhar Gaeilge. Ceist amháin inniu. (Your Irish copybook. One question today.)
structure.content: Candidate box (Ainm, Rang, Mo scéal · chapter · page, N focal liom féin). Examiner box with today's question in full. One ruled line showing yesterday's answer opening with its margin note. Button: Freagair. Nothing else. The next question is chosen by chapter order: Q001 to Q021 first for everyone, then the chapter the pupil's year group is on.

structure.purposeLine: Freagair i do chuid focal féin. Scríobh, ansin abair. (Answer in your own words. Write it, then say it.)
structure.content: Examiner box with the question. Ruled lines where the pupil writes in biro blue, two to four lines expected. Beneath the lines, a strip of six suggested words drawn from the vocabulary group that matches the question's Context (the three context strings are identical in questions.json and vocab.json; the finer topic-to-group map, 12 question topics to about 20 vocab groups, is an hour's hand work). For a blank-slot question (there are 8, for example Q106 "Cad é an rud is mó a thaitníonn leat faoi __________?"), the slot is filled with the pupil's own townland from their profile before it is shown. For a yes/no question (79 of 270) the strip offers reason openers from the 27 opinion phrases and 30 connectives already in the list (mar, mar gheall ar, is dóigh liom go, ar an lámh eile). On Seiceáil the pen marks within a second, in the margin only: a tick beside each line that contains at least one list word; "fada?" with the correct form where a word is a fada away from a list word; a mutation note from the existing engine wherever ar an, sa, leis an, mo, do or an precedes a known noun ("séimhiú: sa charr"); "cad chuige?" beside a yes/no answer with no reason word; "ard." beside an answer of three lines or more with a connective. Then the record button: one press, the pupil says the answer once, plays it back once. The page is saved as page N of the chapter. Words the pupil used that are in the list, and any new word they typed that is not (their club, surname, pet), go into Mo chuid focal; a new word asks one question before it is saved: "Cad é an Béarla air?" and, for a noun, "fear nó bean?" for gender.

structure.purposeLine: Na focail a d'úsáid tú féin. Cuimhnigh orthu. (The words you used yourself. Remember them.)
structure.content: The existing SessionView, unchanged in mechanism (English shown, Irish typed, Leitner boxes 0 to 30 days, wrong ones come round again in the same round) but fed only from the pupil's personal list. Each card carries its provenance line: "ó: Déan cur síos ar do sheomra leapa" and the pupil's own sentence with the word blanked. Five words a round. Verbs still demand root and verbal noun (358 GCSE verbs carry both). The page count in the candidate box is the personal list size, not 2,233.

structure.screen: Gramadach (my words in the right form)
structure.purposeLine: Do chuid focal féin, san fhoirm cheart. (Your own words, in the right form.)
structure.content: The existing Ulster mutation engine (article; ar an, leis an, ag an, as an, faoin, don, ón, chuig an, sa) applied to the nouns in the pupil's own answers, plus mo, do and a from the KS3 framework's possessive list once added to the engine. Question form is the pupil's own sentence with the mutated noun blanked: "Tá mé i mo chónaí i ________ (Béal Átha an Airgid)", "Imrím peil leis an ________ (club)". Diagnosis by rule as now (urú, ní séimhiú; séimhiú de dhíth; t- de dhíth). Three items a round. Pupil-entered nouns with no gender are skipped until the pupil or teacher tags them.

structure.purposeLine: Ceisteanna a d'fhreagair tú cheana, gan an leathanach. (Questions you have already answered, without the page.)
structure.content: The cold run. Only questions the pupil has answered are drawn. The question is shown in the examiner box; the pupil's written answer is hidden; the pupil records from memory; then the page is revealed beside the new recording and the old one, and the pupil marks themselves with one tap: tick (said it), or arís (again), which brings the question back tomorrow. Optional 30-second countdown, off by default (condition 2). When Abair audio arrives, the question is heard rather than read. Three questions a run. This is the KS3 "unprepared speech" and the GCSE conversation in one screen.

structure.purposeLine: Do scéal, caibidil ar chaibidil. (Your story, chapter by chapter.)
structure.content: Reached from the candidate box. The 12 topics as chapter headings in bank order, each with "8 de 21" in biro; tap a chapter to read its pages in order, each page being the question, the pupil's answer on ruled lines, the margin marks, and a play button for the recording. Two actions at the foot: Cuir ceist eile leis (add a question of your own, for the pupil's teacher's favourites) and Priontáil (export the chapter or the whole copybook as a PDF in the exam-script layout, without the recordings, to hand to the teacher or to revise from). Settings (name, class, year, townland, club, strict fadas) live behind the name cell of the candidate box, not in a tab.

concepts.dailyLoop: Five minutes, 8.30 on a school night. Open the app: the home page shows one question, "Cad é an cineál tí atá agat?", chapter Mo cheantar, page 4, and under the button "3 fhocal le cuimhneamh ar dtús". Tap Freagair. (1) Sixty seconds: three of the pupil's own words from earlier pages come up one at a time, English shown, Irish typed, tick or correction in the margin, a wrong one comes back at the end of the three. (2) The question page opens. The pupil reads the question, writes two or three lines in biro: "Tá mé i mo chónaí i dteach scoite. Tá sé mór agus tá gairdín againn." Two minutes, using two of the six suggested words under the lines. (3) Tap Seiceáil. Within a second: a tick beside each line, "gairdín ✓" beside the new word, and one note, "fada? scoite" if they missed one. The pupil fixes it or leaves it. (4) Tap record, say the answer once, twenty to thirty seconds, hear it back once. (5) Tap Críochnaigh. The page turns: the candidate box now reads "lch 5 · 104 focal liom féin", and the home page shows tomorrow's question already printed. Nothing else is asked. On a night the pupil has ten minutes, the home page offers one more line, "An comhrá: 3 cheist ó na leathanaigh a rinne tú", but never demands it.
concepts.register: Keep it, with one rule that changes what it is: the exam script is the pupil's script. The register was chosen as decoration of the app's screens; it has to become the physical form of the pupil's portfolio, so that every ruled line carries the pupil's own writing and the red pen only ever writes beside something the pupil wrote. Where the current proof of concept breaks this, it reads as a costume: the home page prints statistics on ruled lines with a "maith ✓" pen mark next to nothing; the index and topic pages are system Lists with a candidate box stuck on top; the "Aonad 1, 2, 3" numbering imitates a paper without meaning anything. What it must do on each screen: on the home page, the candidate box names the pupil and the chapter, and the only ruled line is yesterday's real answer with its real mark; on the answer page, the examiner box holds the question in the bank's exact wording, the ruled lines hold the pupil's biro, the margin holds the marks, and the rubric line is the pupil-facing purpose line rather than a paper instruction; on the recall and grammar pages, the ruled lines hold the pupil's own sentence with the blank, so the drill is visibly a page of their own copybook being re-read; on the conversation page, the lines are hidden (the page turned face down) until the recording is made, which is the register doing the work of "from memory"; on Mo scéal, the chapters are bound pages that can be printed, which is the register becoming the deliverable. Retain: one print face (Atkinson Hyperlegible when licensed into the app), the red margin rule, the digitised hand for every mark, ticks and corrections with no percentages, biro blue for everything the pupil writes including their name in the box. Drop: the score cell in the candidate box on every page except the marked results page; the tab bar (five system tabs are what made the first mock-up look designed by AI, and the exam script has no tabs; navigation is the candidate box and the one button).
concepts.adhd: The angle and the fork pull the same way. One question per page, and the question is about the pupil's own dog, club or bedroom, which is the most salient content available and does not have to be held in mind because it is already known; the only new thing to hold is the Irish for it. Immediate marked feedback comes within a second of Seiceáil, in the margin, in a real hand, and is about their sentence, not a generic model. The session is five items or one page, never a queue: the home page shows one question, and the count of due words is capped at three before an answer. Predictable structure: every page has the same candidate box, the same purpose line in the same place, the same ruled lines, the same button in the same corner; the answer page, recall page and grammar page are all the same page at different stages of being written. Progress is visible within minutes: the page number and the personal word count rise on the candidate box on every screen in the same session. Re-tests inside a session are kept from the current Session model (a wrong word returns at the end of the round); spacing defaults shorten to 0, 1, 2, 4, 7, 14 days for the personal list, since the list is small and the words are theirs. No streak, no timer unless the cold run is switched on, no red on the home page. One thing the fork adds to the angle: the record button is a second route into the same content for a pupil who will not write three lines but will say them; a spoken-only page is saved as a page with no lines and gets its own tick.
cuts: The Innéacs tab (IndexView.swift): browsing 2,233 words by topic or 826 by band is a dictionary, and the proposal already ruled dictionaries out; it is also the biggest source of the 'what is this for' problem, since it shows the pupil the whole syllabus with a learned count against it.
Generic recall from the whole stage list on the home page (HomeView: flow = SessionFlowRequest(scope: store.items) over 'Gach topaic'). Recall draws only from the pupil's own words.

Random grammar questions drawn from any gendered noun in the list (GrammarQuestion.random(from: nouns) in Grammar.swift). Grammar is set on nouns from the pupil's own pages, in the pupil's own sentence.
The five-item tab bar in CuimhneApp.swift (Inniu, Innéacs, Gramadach, Labhairt, Socruithe). Navigation becomes the candidate box plus the one button; settings move behind the name cell.
Streak, sessionsToday, lastScore and the 'maith ✓' pen mark on the home page; the learned-out-of-total line; the 'Aonad 1/2/3' cells in the candidate box.
The score in the candidate box on every page. It stays only on the marked results page at the end of a round.

The Labhairt topic list and question list as plain SwiftUI Lists (SpeakingView.swift). Questions are never chosen from a list of 270; the next unanswered one in the chapter is served, and answered ones are read back from Mo scéal.
The Stage picker as the primary organiser (SettingsView). Stage becomes an inference from the year group and only changes the suggestion bank and which chapters are served.

The 'Taispeáin dom' reveal on a recall card as a free action. Keep it, but a revealed word is recorded as wrong (it already is) and the pen writes the word into the margin so the reveal reads as a correction.

Data cleaning before any of this ships: the eight legend rows at the tail of the KS3 list (K0819 to K0826, 'pppn = prepositional pronoun' with a count as its English) must go; the 29 KS3 rows with no part of speech and the 1,870 GCSE rows with no gender need the workbook pass the proposal already calls for.
risks: No automatic marking of free prose exists or is proposed. The pen can tick list words, catch a missing fada against a known word, apply the mutation engine after a known trigger, and notice a missing reason word; it cannot say an answer is right. The first-run copy and the purpose line must not promise correction of the whole answer, only notes in the margin. A wrong sentence with the right words gets a tick per line, which a pupil may read as approval.

No model answers. The angle deliberately does without them (the pupil's answer is the model), but a pupil who cannot start needs something. The six suggested words per question and the reason openers from the opinion and connective groups are the substitute; if they are not enough, roughly 300 teacher-checked Ulster model answers are the cost, as the proposal already says.

No audio in either direction. Questions are read, not heard, until Abair's Ulster voice is wired in, so listening is untrained; recordings are heard back only by the pupil. Any speech marking depends on Abair recognition, which is unproven for this use.

Pupil-entered nouns (townland, club, surname, pet) arrive with no gender and no genitive, and place names take eclipsis after 'i' (i mBéal Átha an Airgid) which the engine does not yet do. Grammar on personal nouns needs the possessive and 'i' rules added and a gender tag from the pupil or teacher; until then those nouns are skipped in grammar.

Mapping the 12 question topics to the roughly 20 GCSE vocabulary groups is by hand and not yet done; only the three Contexts match by string today. Without the finer map the suggestion strip is too broad.

The 270 questions are GCSE questions. Years 8 to 10 can use the 21 'Mé féin' questions and many of the 79 yes/no ones, but a Key Stage 3 chapter list needs the Irish department to pick and possibly simplify, and the framework's 'placeholders for a placename and the pupil's surname' are in the framework document, not in vocab.json (only 'ainm' at K0163 is there).

No teacher view. The copybook is private to the device; the only route to the teacher is the printed PDF. This is a feature for privacy and a limit for the department. Recordings of children stay on device and must never sync anywhere without a decision by the school.

Copyright and naming. Questions are shown in the bank's exact wording, which is the point, and the app never names the source; whether verbatim reuse of about 300 questions inside a distributed app is acceptable to the board is the same permissions question the proposal raised for the word list.

Pupils can type English, copy from a friend's copybook, or write one word per page. The tick-per-line rule needs a floor (no tick on a line with no Irish list word) and the export makes copying visible to the teacher, but the app cannot police it.

The register condition on typography: the mock-up used Atkinson Hyperlegible and the PoC uses the system font. Shipping the print face needs its licence checked and the font bundled; it is small but it is what makes the page look like the page.

judgements.lens: A 14-year-old in Year 10 at St Paul's who finds Irish hard and has a phone. Two questions only: would I open it a second night, and would I know what it is for without being told.

scores.angle: Mo Scríbhinn: the pupil's own exam script, 270 numbered lines written in advance, everything else in service of the next line
scores.bestIdea: Every item on every screen carries its line reference in the margin (L38 beside clár), and the answer key for recall is my own earlier line, so I can always see why I am being asked and the app has content without model answers.
scores.weakestPoint: Six items a night (rewrite a line, three words, a grammar form, write a new one-to-three-sentence answer, record it, retest) is ten minutes for me, not five, and a fresh sentence every night is the hardest thing you could ask a pupil who finds Irish hard to do.

scores.angle: Cóipleabhar: five minutes a night built first for ADHD, no home screen, opening is starting
scores.bestIdea: There is no home screen and no start button: the app opens on tonight's page with line 1 live and the keyboard up, wrong lines are rewritten under Ceartúcháin before the page closes, and after 45 seconds of nothing the pen gives the first letter.
scores.weakestPoint: Nothing tells me what the pages add up to. Leathanach amháin, cúig nóiméad says how long, not what for; the window, then the town, then ar an bhord is a vocab quiz and I would not see the exam or myself in it.

scores.angle: Peann Dearg: the teacher's red pen at home marking one page a night
scores.bestIdea: Mo chuid botún, the pen's own back page of things it has corrected twice, written entirely in the hand and crossed out rather than deleted once right three pages running; and the rule that red on any screen is the pen and nothing else.
scores.weakestPoint: It is the same five-line page as the copybook concept but with a total at the foot (4/5) that breaks its own no-score rule, and on my first bad night I get five red crosses in the school's marking colour. The pen is how it works, not a reason to open it.

scores.angle: Bealach: the road from Year 8 to GCSE as nine rows on the booklet's marks grid
scores.bestIdea: The marker's grid on the front cover as the one place progress lives, with a row signed off by a dated tick in the hand instead of a bar or a ring.
scores.weakestPoint: Céim 1 is sixty function words that cannot be drilled from an English prompt, and the cover shows me nine rows spanning five years with 41 as 117 on the live one. That is the syllabus with a queue on it, which is exactly what makes me close the app.

scores.angle: Mo Ghlór: the pupil's own copybook of answers about their own life, with all drill drawn from what they wrote
scores.bestIdea: The question is about my own dog, club and townland, with the blank-slot questions filled from my profile, and the recall and grammar items re-read my own sentence with the word blanked, so the drill is visibly a page of my copybook.
scores.weakestPoint: There is nothing in the app until I write, and writing two to four free lines of Irish is the thing I cannot do. In week one the personal word list is nearly empty, so the recall round has nothing to ask and the app is a blank page with a red pen waiting.

judgements.winner: Mo Scríbhinn (concept 1), with the opening mechanics of Cóipleabhar (concept 2) grafted on and the nightly page cut from six items to four.
judgements.rationale:
Judged as a pupil, the two questions pull in different directions and concept 1 is the only one that answers both. On the first screen I see a cover that says my exam, written by me in advance, a line count (Líne 37 de 270, or de 86 for my year), tonight's actual question on the ruled lines, and last night's one correction in red. I know what it is for without being told, and I know what tonight is. Every later screen keeps that thread: a word in the index or a grammar form on the daily page says in the margin which line of my script it belongs to, so nothing feels like a random quiz. That is the thing the principal said was missing and no other concept carries it as far; concepts 2 and 3 have a consistent look (a copybook, a red pen) but the look explains the mechanism, not the point, and I would call either of them a vocab quiz app. Concept 4 is clear but reads as a five-year syllabus with a counter, and concept 5 is clear and personal but empty until I write, which is the thing I find hardest.

Concept 1's weakness is the second question: would I open it again. Six items with a fresh sentence and a recorded reading every night is not five minutes for me, and the concept's own five-minute promise is the kind of thing I stop believing on night three. So the synthesis should keep the script as the data structure and the line reference in every margin, but take from concept 2 the mechanics that make me come back: open straight onto tonight's page with line 1 live and the keyboard up, no Scríobh button; a first-letter hint after a stall; corrections rewritten at the foot before the page closes; a small Leathanach eile link, never a queue. Cut the daily page to four items (rewrite one line, two words, one grammar form, then either a new line or a spoken retelling of an old one, alternating nights), so a new sentence is asked every second night, not every night. From concept 3 take the rule that red is the pen only and the Mo chuid botún page; from concept 5 take filling the blank-slot questions with my own townland and club. Leave concept 4's grid alone: a pupil who finds Irish hard does not want to see the road.

Two cautions carried over. First, all five concepts promise marking of free sentences that the data cannot deliver; the ? for unknown words and never a cross is the right rule and the first-run text must not overpromise. Second, none of the copybook concepts survive the first bad night if the page ends in five red crosses, so the closing comment and the retest inside the page matter more than any of the concept text admits.

judgements.lens: Head of Irish at St Paul's: does it move marks in the speaking, writing and reading papers, does it fit the Key Stage 3 framework (recall, writing from memory, unprepared speech, personal vocabulary), and can I stand over every word of Irish on the screen.

scores.angle: 1. Mo Scríbhinn: the pupil's own exam script, written in advance over two years
scores.bestIdea: The pupil's own earlier line is the answer key: a written answer comes back at 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 days to be rewritten from memory and marked word by word against itself, and every drill item (word, grammar form) prints its line reference (L38) in the margin so the pupil always sees why they are being asked. That is the only concept in which the vocabulary, the grammar and the speaking are visibly one thing, and it is buildable today without a single authored model answer.
scores.weakestPoint: The nightly page is too heavy for the pupil it claims to serve first: a rewrite from memory, three words, a grammar form, a new line of one to three sentences and a recording is two free-writing tasks a night, nearer eight minutes than five for a Year 9 with ADHD. And nothing in the app can tell a pupil their line is bad Irish; the printed page for the teacher is the only correction, so a wrong sentence written in Year 8 is rehearsed faithfully until Year 12 unless a teacher marks paper. The word-level ticking of free text through séimhiú, urú, plurals and genitive will miss more than it catches.

scores.angle: 2. Cóipleabhar: five minutes a night, built first for the pupil with ADHD
scores.bestIdea: Open on the live line with the keyboard up and the fada row fixed above it, and put Ceartúcháin at the foot of the page: the wrong word or form written out again by the pupil before the page can close. That is exactly what a marked copybook at St Paul's looks like, it is the in-session retest the ADHD ruling asked for, and it costs nothing to build.
scores.weakestPoint: It answers what to do, not what it is for. 'Leathanach amháin. Cúig nóiméad.' is an instruction; the exam, the questions and the reason for the words appear only in the first-run text and at the back of the book. The principal's complaint ('nothing running through the app explaining what it is for') survives this concept intact. Three words a night is 50 to 60 words a month against a 2,233 list, so it forms a habit and moves few marks. Also 'cúig nóiméad' where the school says 'bomaite'.

scores.angle: 3. Peann Dearg: the teacher's red pen at home
scores.bestIdea: Mo chuid botún: a back page, written in the hand, of the words and forms the pen has had to correct twice, grouped by fault (fada, séimhiú, urú ní séimhiú, ainm briathartha), crossed out rather than deleted when right three pages running. That is the error log that moves writing-paper marks, and it falls straight out of the diagnoses Grammar.swift already produces. The rule 'if it is red, the teacher wrote it' is the second thing worth taking.
scores.weakestPoint: The purpose line ('a real teacher's red pen marks it straight away') claims something the app cannot do. The marking of the written answer is list lookup, fada check and nine prepositions, dressed in a named teacher's hand; a pupil will read the pen's silence on an unknown word as approval, and a parent will take '5/6, na fadaí, a Aoife' as a teacher's assessment. The front page also carries '4/5' in the margin every morning, which is a score by another name against the no-percentages ruling. Cén bhliain, not cad é an bhliain, in the cover copy.

scores.angle: 4. Bealach: the road from Year 8 to Year 12, made visible
scores.bestIdea: The marks grid on the front cover of an answer booklet as the home screen, one row per stop, ticked and dated in the hand when earned. It is the one register-native answer to 'where am I' that no other concept has, and a version with three rows (the three GCSE contexts) rather than nine would sit on the cover of concept 1's script without harm.
scores.weakestPoint: The arithmetic and the data both fail it. 2,233 GCSE words at five a night is 446 school nights; Céim 1 is 60 function words (an, agus, ar, na) that cannot be drilled from an English prompt; the grammar pages for stops 2 to 9 do not exist because the engine covers the article and nine prepositions only; and the general words have no stop. Showing a Year 8 nine rows and a Year 11 six unsigned rows above them is the long queue up front that the ADHD ruling forbids, and it keeps the 30-day interval, 'aréir 4/5' and 'Babhta eile'. 'Scrúdú fuar' is a calque of 'cold exam' that no pupil would say.

scores.angle: 5. Mo Ghlór: the pupil's own Irish voice; nothing appears that the pupil did not write
scores.bestIdea: The provenance line under every drill item ('ó: Déan cur síos ar do sheomra leapa' with the pupil's own sentence and the word blanked), and grammar set on the pupil's own nouns inside the pupil's own sentence ('Tá mé i mo chónaí i ________'). Together with the spoken-only page for a pupil who will say three lines but not write them, that is the strongest ADHD idea in any of the five.
scores.weakestPoint: The list is never taught. Recall draws only from words the pupil has already produced, so a Year 11 who writes short answers meets almost none of the 2,233 words the listening and reading papers draw on, and the first fortnight of recall is nearly empty. It needs the untested topic-to-group map, a gender tag on every personal noun, and eclipsis after 'i' before the grammar works on the pupil's townland. The Irish needs a hand on it: Béal Átha an Airgid is Silverbridge, not Bessbrook (An Sruthán); 'fear nó bean?' is not how gender is asked (firinscneach nó baininscneach); 'ard.' means nothing to a pupil; and the KS3 chapters are left for the department to pick.

judgements.winner: 1. Mo Scríbhinn: the pupil's own exam script
judgements.rationale: Concept 1 wins on the two things the principal actually complained about and the thing I answer for. Its first screen says the end (Do scrúdú, scríofa agat roimh ré), the means (tonight's actual question on the ruled lines) and the standing (Líne 37 de 270); no other concept states purpose on the first screen without a tour. Its thread is structural rather than a persona: every word and grammar form carries the line of the script it serves, so the pupil never meets an item with no reason. And it is the only concept whose nightly loop directly produces the thing the speaking paper rewards (a prepared personal answer to each of the 270 questions) while also doing what the Key Stage 3 framework names (writing from memory, unprepared speech in the cold exam, a personal vocabulary, regular recall), using the pupil's own earlier line as the answer key so it needs no authored model answers to start. It is not the best fit for the ADHD fork as written: the six-item page must be cut to four (rewrite, two words, new line) and the recording made optional, which is concept 2's discipline. Concept 3 ties on paper but its purpose line promises marking the app cannot do, and as head of Irish I will not put a named teacher's hand on spell-check-grade marks of free prose without the printed page going to a real marker. Grafts, in order: concept 2's open-on-the-live-line and Ceartúcháin foot; concept 3's Mo chuid botún page and the red-is-the-pen-only rule; concept 5's provenance line (concept 1's L38 does half of it) and spoken-only page; concept 4's cover grid reduced to the three contexts. Concepts 4 and 5 lose because they do not fit the data that exists: 4 needs grammar pages and a road the arithmetic cannot finish, 5 has no content until the pupil writes and never exposes the list. Preconditions for any of them, which the winner shares: the workbook cleaning pass (feminine gender in the GCSE list, the 29 junk rows in the KS3 list), an English gloss on each of the 270 questions, checking the hand font for fadas, ticks and an apostrophe, and Ulster sign-off on every line of copy (bomaite not nóiméad, cad é not cén, An Sruthán for Bessbrook).

judgements.lens: Product designer who has seen a thousand language apps and rejects anything generic. Two questions asked of every screen: does one idea run through it, and is the exam-script register doing structural work or dressing a drill.

scores.angle: Mo Scríbhinn: the pupil's own exam script, 270 numbered lines written in advance, everything else in the app exists to make the next line possible
scores.bestIdea: The pupil's own earlier line is the answer key for recall, and every item on every screen prints in the margin which line of the script it belongs to (L38 beside clár). That is the one mechanism in the five that makes a word drill, a grammar item and a recording all visibly serve the same object, and it needs no authored content.
scores.weakestPoint: The daily page is over-packed: six items including a free-written line and a recording in five minutes is not five minutes for the pupil this is meant for, and Líne 37 de 270 on the cover is a 270-deep queue shown up front to a Year 8 whose exam is four years away. The concept is right that the script is the data structure; it has not yet cut the page down to what the fork can carry.

scores.angle: Cóipleabhar: five minutes a night built first for the pupil with ADHD; no home screen, opening is starting, five lines in a fixed order, corrections at the foot, close
scores.bestIdea: Open the app onto the live line with the keyboard up and the fada row fixed, no Tosaigh button, and after about 45 seconds of nothing typed the pen writes the first letter on the line. Plus Ceartúcháin at the foot as the in-session retest in register. These are the best attention decisions in the set and should be grafted whatever wins.
scores.weakestPoint: The thread is a habit, not a purpose. Leathanach amháin, cúig nóiméad tells the pupil what to do and never why; so the words stick is the same promise every flashcard app makes. The principal's complaint was that nothing in the app says what it is for, and this concept answers it with a shape rather than an end. It also shares its page almost line for line with concept three.

scores.angle: Peann Dearg: one copybook marked every night by a real teacher's red pen; the pupil owns the lines, the pen owns the margin
scores.bestIdea: Red is the pen and nothing else: if it is red, the teacher wrote it, and the pen writes only what a teacher writes on a page (tick, cross, ?, the right form, a note of two to six words, a total, a one-line comment). Together with Mo chuid botún, a back page written entirely in the hand listing what has been corrected twice, and the rule that a wrong word gets ? in grey print rather than a red cross. This is the discipline that makes the register serve instead of decorate and it applies to every concept.
scores.weakestPoint: The pen is a persona that overpromises. A real teacher's red pen marks it straight away is the purpose line, and the marking behind it is spell-check against a list plus nine preposition rules. The concept knows this (scríofa and the grey ?) but the promise on the front page is still one the app cannot keep on the item that matters most, the written answer, and a parent will read a dated 5/6 in the principal's hand as an assessment.

scores.angle: Bealach: the road from Year 8 to GCSE made visible as a nine-row marks grid on the booklet cover, one row per frequency band or context, filled in over five years
scores.bestIdea: The marks grid on the front cover of an answer booklet as the home screen, and the road line in red at the end of every task (Céim 3: 41 → 44 as 117). It is the register's own furniture for progress and it is the only concept that gives the cover a native non-task form. Worth grafting as one small line, not as the organising idea.
scores.weakestPoint: It is the unit map of every language app in exam-booklet clothing, and it breaks on its own data: Céim 1 is 76 function words that cannot be drilled by English-to-Irish typing, 2,233 GCSE words at five a night is 446 nights, eight of the nine grammar pages do not exist, and the year-to-stop mapping is a guess. For the ADHD fork it puts a 3,000-word queue on the first screen, which is the thing the ruling forbids.

scores.angle: Mo Ghlór: the pupil's own Irish voice; nothing appears in the app that did not come from a page the pupil wrote, the 270 questions are the chapter headings of their own story
scores.bestIdea: The provenance line under every drilled item (ó: Cá bhfuil tú i do chónaí? with the pupil's own sentence, the word blanked) and the rule that if there is nothing of the pupil's to put on the ruled lines, the lines are not drawn. That rule alone would have caught every fault in the proof of concept's home screen.
scores.weakestPoint: The app is empty until the pupil writes, and it only ever drills words the pupil has already produced, so the high-frequency spine the framework is built on is bypassed: a pupil who can write 90 words will be tested on 90 words for ever. It also asks the pupil this is for to write two to four lines of free prose every night, the hardest task available, with no gender on their own nouns, no topic-to-group map, and no Key Stage 3 chapter list.

judgements.rationale:
The principal's complaint is that nothing runs through the app saying what it is for. Only one concept answers that with a structure rather than a slogan: in Mo Scríbhinn the exam script is not a visual register over a drill, it is the data model. A page is a page, a line is a line, a mark is a mark, and the purpose (Do scrúdú, scríofa agat roimh ré) is the rubric on the first screen every night. The line reference in the margin of every item is the thread made visible: a pupil doing a word or a grammar form can always see which line of their own script it feeds. It also passes the printing test, which is the cleanest test of whether the register decorates: the cover, a topic page, a line and the index could each be handed to a teacher as a page of a candidate's script. Its answer key for recall is the pupil's own earlier writing, which is the one thing that exists today without model answers.

Peann Dearg runs it close and is the more disciplined about the register (red is the pen only, the pen writes only what a teacher writes) but its thread is a voice, and the voice promises marking the data cannot deliver. Cóipleabhar is the best ADHD design in the set and the weakest on purpose. Mo Ghlór is the most distinctive and the worst fit for the data and the framework. Bealach is the only one that covers the lists and it is generic to the bone.

The synthesis should take Mo Scríbhinn as the spine and graft: from Cóipleabhar, open onto the live line with no start button, the 45-second first-letter hint, and Ceartúcháin at the foot; from Peann Dearg, the red-is-the-pen rule, the grey ? for unknown words, scríofa when the pen has nothing to say, and Mo chuid botún; from Mo Ghlór, no ruled line without the pupil's writing on it; from Bealach, one road line at the close of the page. Then cut Mo Scríbhinn's daily page from six items to five (the rewrite, three words, either the grammar form or the new line, not both every night, so the free-written line falls every second night) and drop the 270 denominator for Years 8 to 10: the cover shows the current topic page's count (Líne 12 de 21), never the whole script. Rename: Cuimhne names a means; the name should name the object.

All three lenses ranked it first (23, 24, 24) and the pupil and the Irish teacher agree it is the only concept that states its purpose on the first screen without a tour. Grafted with Cóipleabhar's opening mechanics and Peann Dearg's pen discipline, and cut, as all three judges asked, from six items a night to four, with a new line written every second night and a written line said from memory on the other nights.

brief.brief:
# Mo Scríbhinn: the concept brief

## What it is for

Fill one page a night, writing or saying your own exam answers, so on the day nothing is new.

After twenty school nights: ten lines of the pupil's own script in biro, half the first topic page, each rewritten from memory and marked against their own earlier line, each said once and recorded; their listed words ticked in the index; the forms of their own nouns drilled; a page they can print for their teacher.

## The thread

The script. One exam booklet belonging to one candidate: tonight's page at the front, twelve topic pages of numbered lines (270 in all), an index at the back, an inside cover. A line is the pupil's own answer, written on the rules in biro, marked in the margin in the principal's red hand, said once in their own voice, rewritten from memory at widening intervals until it is theirs. Everything else exists to make the next line possible or the last line better.

On every screen: the candidate box carries Ainm, Rang, the sitting and the standing on the current page (Líne 12 de 21), never a score, never 270; one italic rubric is the only heading; every item prints its line reference in the margin (L12); only the pupil's biro goes on a rule; red is the pen alone; the foot carries one action; no tab bar.

## First open

Irish: Seo do scríbhinn féin. Ar na leathanaigh seo tá na ceisteanna a chuirfeas an scrúdaitheoir ort. Achan oíche líonfaidh tú leathanach amháin: scríobhfaidh tú líne i do chuid focal féin, nó déarfaidh tú líne a scríobh tú cheana. Marcálfaidh mise é sa chiumhais leis an pheann dhearg. Faoi lá an scrúdaithe ní bheidh rud ar bith le rá agat den chéad uair. Cúig bhomaite san oíche, sin an méid.

English: This is your own exam script. On these pages are the questions the examiner will ask you. Every night you fill one page: you write a line in your own words, or you say a line you have already written. I mark it in the margin in red pen. By exam day there will be nothing you have to say for the first time. Five minutes a night, that is all.

In print, not the hand.

## Home

No home apart from the work: the app opens on tonight's page. The rubric reads, every night, Do scrúdú, scríofa agat roimh ré (Your exam, written by you in advance). It shows the standing (Líne 12 de 21), last night's note in the margin in the hand (ó aréir: sa charr), and item 1 live with the keyboard up. The one action: write on line 1.

## The screens

**1. Leathanach an lae (tonight's page).** Rubric: Do scrúdú, scríofa agat roimh ré. Four items in a fixed order, one live. 1 Athscríobh: a due line rewritten from memory, marked word by word against the pupil's own saved line. 2 Focal: a word missed in item 1, else one from the current page's list not yet in any line, else a due word. 3 Foirm: an article or preposition form from a noun of known gender in the pupil's own lines, diagnosed by rule. 4 Líne: odd pages Líne nua, the next unwritten question, one to three sentences, ticks on listed words, a grey ? on unlisted words, never a cross, cad chuige? beside an opinion with no mar; even pages Abair é, a written line said from memory, page face down, recorded, revealed, self-marked. Ceartúcháin: anything crossed is written out again. Close: the date, 4 thic, ceartú amháin, Mé féin: 12 de 21, Sin é anocht.

**2. An scríbhinn.** Rubric: Gach a ndéarfaidh tú ar lá an scrúdaithe, i do chuid focal féin. Twelve topic pages under three contexts, each its questions as numbered lines, blank or in biro with red marks and a date; Críochnaithe across a finished page; Priontáil an leathanach; Scrúdú béil from ten written lines.

**3. Líne.** Rubric: the question. The answer in biro, earlier drafts crossed through and dated beneath, the recording, Athscríobh ó chuimhne; a word marked ? joins Mo chuid focal féin.

**4. Innéacs.** Rubric: Na focail atá de dhíth ar do scríbhinn, agus cé acu atá agat. One list per topic page, a tick in the hand where a word has been written in a line and recalled. Last pages: Mo chuid focal féin, Mo chuid botún in the hand.

**5. Scrúdú béil.** Rubric: Mar a bheas sé ar an lá: ceist gan choinne, gan do scríbhinn os do chomhair. Five random questions from written pages, the only countdown; answer aloud, line revealed, one-tap self-mark.

**6. An clúdach istigh.** Rubric: Cé thú féin agus cá huair a bheas an scrúdú. Name, class, exam month, the candidate's own topic pages, townland and club, strict fadas, print, clear, a print line saying the marking is automatic. The exam date sets the pace.

## A school night in five minutes

8.30. Aoife, 10B: Líne 12 de 21, in the margin ó aréir: sa charr. Item 1: Athscríobh, L4, Cá mhéad deartháir atá agat? She writes it from memory; ticks on each matching word, the missing amháin in red. Item 2: amháin, tick. Item 3: sa + carr from L11; she types sa carr: cross, sa charr in red above, séimhiú de dhíth. Item 4, an even page: Abair é, L7. Page face down, she says her line, reveals it, ticks it. Ceartúcháin: sa charr once. The pen writes the date, 4 thic, ceartú amháin, Mé féin: 12 de 21, Sin é anocht.

## The exam-script register, what it must do

Keep it, made literal: the script is the data structure, not a skin. The proof of concept decorated non-script: statistics on rules, Aonad labels, scores in the box, a Sampla sentence, a tab bar. On every screen: the candidate box carries standing, never a score; the rubric is the one heading; a rule carries only the pupil's biro, and a rule nobody writes on is not drawn; the margin carries marks in the hand and line references in print; red is the pen only, and the pen writes nothing a teacher would not write; the foot carries one action. The test: could the screen be printed and handed to a teacher as a page of a candidate's script.

## For a pupil with ADHD

Progress is an object: lines appear in biro, a page fills, Críochnaithe is written across it. The same four items in the same order every night, one live at a time; the queue is never shown; the count is the current page, never 270. Marking is instant; a wrong item is written out again before the page closes. Boxes of 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 days. The page closes itself; more is only a small link. No streak, no timer except the cold exam; the closing comment kind and about a named thing. Atkinson Hyperlegible at 20 point, keyboard up, fada row fixed.

## What comes out of the current build

The five-tab TabView. HomeView's statistics, streak, lastScore and maith tick. The score slot in ExamHeader. The Aonad labels. GrammarView as an endless drill, its rule box, the gender default of m. IndexView as a browse with learned counts. SpeakingView's three-level list. ResultsView and Babhta eile. SettingsView's Form and stage picker. Intervals 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 30. The free Taispeáin dom reveal. The name Cuimhne.

## What has to be true before it can be built

Data: the workbook cleaning pass (feminine gender in the topic list); a twelve-row table from question topics to vocabulary groups; an English gloss on each of the 270 questions; the script kept in files with iCloud sync before any Year 8 starts. Audio: none to start; the Abair Ulster voice is needed to hear a question in the cold exam and for phonics. Model answers: none to start, since the pupil's own earlier line is the key; but the app cannot say a line is good Irish, so the printed page to the teacher is the correction route until authored answers exist. The hand has no apostrophe, so pen phrases avoid it and a length limit sits in code. Every line of Irish signed off for Ulster form by a named teacher.
