grafted: From Cóipleabhar (concept 2): the app opens on the live line with the keyboard up and no start button; the first-letter hint after 45 seconds idle; Ceartúcháin at the foot of the page as the in-session retest in register; Leathanach eile as a small link never shown before the page is done; the class number choosing the word spine silently; function words excluded as recall prompts.

From Peann Dearg (concept 3): red is the pen and nothing else; the pen writes only what a teacher writes and nothing longer than a few words; a grey print ? for unknown words, never a red cross; the closing comment names the thing (sa charr arís amárach); Mo chuid botún, the back page in the hand of forms corrected twice, crossed out after three right pages; the inside cover stating the marking is automatic.

From Mo Ghlór (concept 5): no ruled line is drawn unless the pupil's own writing goes on it; the eight blank-slot questions filled from the pupil's townland and club; the spoken route (Abair é) as a full item for a pupil who will say a line but not write one; a ? word added to the personal vocabulary from the line it appeared in.

From Bealach (concept 4): one road line in the hand at the close of every page (Mé féin: 12 de 21) and the three contexts as the contents headings of the script; the nine-row grid itself is not taken.

From the three judges jointly: the daily page cut from six items to four, with a new line written every second night and a written line said from memory on the other nights; the candidate box counts the current topic page (de 21), never 270.
openQuestionsForPrincipal: Which topic pages a candidate is expected to hold in the script for the conversation: all twelve, or the pages the pupil or their teacher ticks on the inside cover. This sets the denominator on the candidate box and the pace the exam date computes, and it is the difference between a Year 12 who starts in February being shown one line a night or four.

Whether the printed page is the marking route: a teacher marks the paper page by hand and the pupil writes the correction into the app, which is the only correction of bad Irish the concept has until model answers exist. If yes, the printed page is the first thing that leaves the device, and the school's decision on what may leave it (print only, or later a teacher view) should be made before the print button is built.

Who signs off every line of Irish in the app and the pen's stock phrases in his hand: himself or a named Irish teacher. The copy in this brief uses bomaite, achan, cad é and leis an pheann dhearg on that assumption, and the pen speaks as mise, so the sign-off also decides whether the marks are presented as his.

critiques.lens: A 14-year-old in Year 10 at St Paul's who finds Irish hard, has a phone, and is asking two things: would I open it a second time, and would I know what it is for without being told.

problems.problem: The thread is written in the language I find hard. The brief makes the italic rubric the only heading and drops the English gloss the proof of concept's Rubric(ga:en:) already carried. 'Do scrúdú, scríofa agat roimh ré', 'Athscríobh', 'Foirm', 'Ceartúcháin', 'ó aréir: sa charr' mean nothing to me on night one. The principal's complaint was that nothing runs through the app explaining what it is for; a rubric I cannot read does not fix that, it moves the problem into Irish.
problems.fix: Keep the exam papers' own convention: every rubric has its English beneath in smaller print (Rubric(ga:en:) stays). Each of the four items carries a one-line print instruction under its label: 'Athscríobh: write your line 4 again from memory', 'Focal: one word from your page', 'Foirm: the right form after sa', 'Líne nua: your answer to question 12'. The pen phrases (séimhiú de dhíth, cad chuige?) stay Irish-only because a teacher would write them so, but a tap on any pen phrase shows its print gloss once.

problems.problem: In Year 10 I have no speaking exam and no exam month. The inside cover asks for one and 'Do scrúdú' is the nightly heading, but yearGroup 8 to 10 draws on the frequency list, which has no questions at all (it is 826 words with no question bank). For me the script is 270 questions written for somebody else's exam and the pace calculation divides by school nights to a date I do not have.
problems.fix: Be honest that the script is a GCSE booklet. For Years 8 to 10, the inside cover asks for the date of the next class oral or the June assessment instead of exam month, the candidate box reads 'Scrúdú béil: Meitheamh', and the script opens only the first two topic pages (Mé féin, Caitheamh aimsire), whose questions (Cad é an t-ainm atá ort? Cá mhéad deartháir atá agat? An imríonn tú spórt ar bith?) a Year 10 can answer. Focal and Foirm draw from the frequency bands as planned. Do not pretend the frequency list generates a script; it feeds items 2 and 3 only.

problems.problem: The intro says 'every night you fill one page' but the standing says 'Líne 12 de 21', so a page is 21 lines and takes weeks. Two things are both called a page (leathanach an lae and the topic page). And the promise is false anyway: on odd nights I write one new line and on even nights I write nothing new, so twenty school nights give ten lines, as the brief's own outcome paragraph admits.
problems.fix: Reserve 'leathanach' for the topic page. Call the nightly unit 'Anocht' (the rubric already sits under it). Rewrite the intro's third sentence to what actually happens: 'Achan oíche scríobhfaidh tú líne amháin i do chuid focal féin agus déarfaidh tú ceann a scríobh tú cheana' / 'Every night you write one line in your own words and say one you wrote before'. Then make that true: item 4 is always Líne nua and Abair é becomes a short fixed item 5 on the line written two nights earlier (saying a line takes twenty seconds and fits the five minutes).

problems.problem: Red ticks at St Paul's mean 'correct'. Item 4 puts a tick on every listed word, so 'Tá mé ina chónaí i mBessbrook' comes back with three ticks and one grey ? and I read that as right. I then rewrite that wrong line from memory at 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 days, marked against itself, and say it in the exam. The brief knows the app cannot judge a line ('the printed page to the teacher is the correction route') but the screen says the opposite.
problems.fix: The tick is reserved for what the app can actually verify: Athscríobh (matches my own line), Focal (matches the list) and Foirm (rule-checked). On a new line the pen underlines listed words in red instead of ticking them and writes one margin note in the hand: 'ar an liosta' beside the line, with the print gloss 'words from your list; your teacher checks the Irish'. After five new lines on a page the foot action once becomes Priontáil an leathanach so the teacher's real red pen sees the lines before I have rehearsed them ten times.

problems.problem: A page never fills for most of us. Free time has 39 questions, Local area 36, School 33, Part-time jobs 31. At one new line every two nights a 39-line page takes 78 school nights, about four months, before Críochnaithe is written across it. The brief says 'progress is an object: a page fills'; for a pupil with ADHD the object has to fill inside a fortnight or it is not progress, it is a debt. 'Líne 3 de 39' is exactly the long queue the ADHD fork forbids.
problems.fix: Split any topic page over 20 questions into sheets of 10 to 20 lines (1a, 1b) in the fixed question order: Free time into 3, Local area, School and Part-time into 2 each, giving 17 sheets. The candidate box reads 'Líne 3 de 13'. Críochnaithe goes across a sheet; the contents page shows the sheets under their topic with a tick each. With one new line a night a sheet finishes in two to three school weeks.

problems.problem: The first week is 'say your name aloud and record it'. Questions 1 to 7 are one-word answers (name, where you live, how many in the family, brothers, sisters, school, class). Night 2 is Abair é on 'Aoife is ainm dom', page face down, recorded: I would feel stupid and I would not open it a third time.
problems.fix: Until five lines exist on a sheet there is no Abair é. On the first sheet, item 4 asks the one-sentence questions two at a time (Q001 and Q002 on night one, Q003 and Q004 on night two) so the first real line, Déan cur síos ort féin, arrives on night four with seven lines already in biro above it. Abair é begins on night five with five lines to choose from.

problems.problem: The recording in Abair é is decoration. The flow is: page face down, say it, reveal, tick. Nobody plays the recording, nothing marks it, and there is no Irish speech recognition. I am asked to record myself for no visible reason.
problems.fix: Either play the recording back automatically while the revealed line is on screen, so I hear myself against my own text before I self-mark (the reveal button becomes 'Éist agus amharc'), or drop recording from Abair é and keep it in LineView only where the pupil chooses it. Do not keep a microphone step whose output nothing uses.

problems.problem: The cold exam's rubric promises 'Mar a bheas sé ar an lá' but the question is shown in print. On the day the examiner speaks it and I have to catch it by ear. A print question with a countdown is a reading test, not the exam, and the brief lists audio as 'none to start'.
problems.fix: Do not wait for Abair for this. One teacher recording the 270 questions on a phone is about ninety minutes of work and gives an Ulster voice the school already trusts; ship them as 270 m4a files beside questions.json and play the question in the cold exam with the print appearing only after a second tap ('Léigh í'). Until those files exist the rubric must say 'Léigh an cheist' and drop 'Mar a bheas sé ar an lá'.

problems.problem: The cad chuige? trigger set is wrong for the data. The Barúlacha group's 27 entries include dom, mar, mar gheall ar, áfach, b'fhéidir, ina áit sin, os a choinne sin, ar an lámh eile, mise ach oiread and go pearsanta. Written as specified, 'Tabhair dom an leabhar' gets cad chuige? in the margin and a pupil learns that the pen is random.
problems.fix: Trigger cad chuige? only on the fourteen opinion frames: is maith liom, ní maith liom, is fearr liom, is breá liom, is aoibhinn liom, is grá liom, is fuath liom, tá dúil agam i, tá dúil mhór agam i, sílim go/gur, is dóigh liom go/gur, is é mo bharúil go/gur, cuireann sé isteach orm, níl suim dá laghad agam ann; and suppress it when the same sentence or the next contains mar, mar gheall ar, cionn is go or de bhrí go.

problems.problem: The blank-slot fill is wrong for two of the eight. Q093 'Cad é an seomra sa teach ina bhfaigheann tú __________?' and Q094 'An maith leat __________?' are not place slots; filling them from townland or club produces nonsense ('An maith leat Bessbrook?' is plausible but Q093 is not). And 42 questions carry slash alternatives ('Déan cur síos ar do dheartháir/dheirfiúr', 'Cé hé/hí an popcheoltóir/an t-imreoir is fearr leat?', one 153 characters long) that a rubric cannot show as a single question I answer.
problems.fix: Fill Q101 to Q106 from townland as planned (the eclipsis after i(n) stays unmarked as the brief says). Author Q093 and Q094 with the examiner's likely word and have the named teacher sign them off. For the 42 slash questions, the rubric shows the first alternative and a small print 'nó' link that swaps to the other; the pupil's line is saved against the variant shown, and the cold exam asks the variant that was written.

problems.problem: The margin note at the top of tonight's page, 'ó aréir: sa charr', is cryptic to me. It is separated from the item that retests it, so it reads like a code.
problems.fix: Put last night's correction beside the item that carries it tonight (item 2 or 3), written as the pen would: 'sa charr, arís!' with the item beneath. Nothing goes at the top of the page except the rubric and the standing.

problems.problem: Nobody tells me whose hand this is. The intro says 'Marcálfaidh mise é' / 'I mark it in red pen' and never says who 'I' is. The whole point of a real digitised hand is that it is a real person's; without the name it is just a font.
problems.fix: The inside cover, in print, states 'Lámh an Phríomhoide, Dáithí Ó Muirí, atá ar na marcanna. Is í an mheaisín a mharcálann.' / 'The marks are in the Principal's hand. The marking is done by the app.' and the first-open text says 'Marcálfaidh an Príomhoide é' instead of 'mise'. The candidate box on every printed page carries the same line so a teacher knows the red is not theirs.

problems.problem: The intro is shown once and is 100 words. I will not read it on night one and I cannot find it on night twelve when my mate asks what the app is.
problems.fix: The intro is the inside cover's own text, permanent, one tap from the contents line at the foot of tonight's page, like the instructions to candidates on the inside of a real exam booklet. On first open the app shows the blank first sheet with all its questions printed on the rules before it asks for line 1: the blank booklet explains the purpose better than the paragraph does.

problems.problem: Three Leitner queues (lines, words, forms) feed one slot each per night. After twenty nights with ten lines, each line is due four times inside sixteen days, so about two rewrites a night fall due and only one is taken. The queue is hidden (good) but the intervals silently stop being the intervals, and the ceartúchán of a wrong three-sentence rewrite means retyping three sentences at the foot of a five-minute page.
problems.fix: Abair é counts as a recall for scheduling so both recall items share one queue and the load halves. Item 1 takes the most overdue line and never more than one; the small link at the foot, not the page, offers a second. Ceartúcháin for a rewrite is the missing or wrong words written once each, not the whole line.

problems.problem: The twelve topic pages have no Irish titles. questions.json carries English topic names ('Myself, my family, relationships and choices') and the vocabulary groups are named differently ('Caitheamh aimsire', 'Dialann an lae'), so the close stamp's 'Mé féin: 12 de 21' and the contents page cannot be produced from the data.
problems.fix: Author twelve short Irish page titles with English beneath (Mé féin agus mo theaghlach; Caitheamh aimsire agus an gnáthlá; Na meáin shóisialta agus an teicneolaíocht; Nósanna agus féilte; Mo cheantar; Cúrsaí sóisialta; Taisteal; An pobal; Mo chuid staidéir; Obair pháirtaimseartha; Imeachtaí iarscoile; Pleananna) as a field in the twelve-row topic table the brief already requires, and have the named teacher sign them off with the rest.

critiques.stillMissing: Two things. First, what a pupil in Years 8 to 10 is preparing for: the script is built from GCSE examiner questions and an exam month, and the frequency list has no questions, so for me the honest answer is 'the June oral and your teacher's printed page', and the brief does not say that anywhere. Second, why I should trust the red pen: the app cannot tell me my line is good Irish, the brief admits it, but nothing on the page says so in words a 14-year-old will read; until the teacher's printed page is the visible end of the loop, the ticks promise a correction the app cannot give.

critiques.lens: Head of Irish: does every word of Irish stand up, does the nightly page move speaking-exam marks rather than writing-paper marks, and does it fit what Years 8 to 10 will be asked to do under the 2028 framework

problems.problem: First open lands the pupil on a blank Líne 1 de 21 with no name in the candidate box, and the only statement of purpose is a nine-line paragraph that is dismissed once and never seen again. 'Marcálfaidh mise é' is spoken by nobody the pupil can identify, and it promises marking the app cannot do: it can tick listed words and correct séimhiú after nine prepositions, it cannot say a line is good Irish.
problems.fix: First open is the inside cover, filled in as a candidate fills a real cover: Ainm, Rang, Scrúdú (month and year), then the two topic pages ticked. Only then tonight's page, with item 4 only and question 1 (Cad é an t-ainm atá ort?), a one-line answer, one tick in the margin: purpose shown inside sixty seconds. Rewrite the paragraph honestly and shorter: 'Seo do scríbhinn féin. Na ceisteanna a chuirfeas an scrúdaitheoir ort, agus do chuid freagraí féin orthu. Cuirfidh an peann dearg tic le achan fhocal ón liosta a úsáideann tú agus ceartóidh sé an séimhiú agus an t-urú. Do mhúinteoir a cheartóidh an chuid eile, ón leathanach a phriontálann tú. Faoi lá an scrúdaithe ní bheidh rud ar bith le rá agat den chéad uair.' Put the exam month permanently in the candidate box (Scrúdú: Bealtaine 2028); that date, not a paragraph, is what carries the purpose night after night.

problems.problem: The whole design trains a candidate to write, but the exam this prepares for is a conversation. Athscríobh (written recall) is item 1 every night; Abair é happens on alternate nights only; the cold exam needs ten written lines first. A pupil who learns three-sentence lines word-perfect on paper recites them on the day and loses marks for interaction and for the follow-up question, which is where the department loses most marks now.
problems.fix: Make the box schedule move a line from paper to voice: boxes 0 and 1 are Athscríobh, boxes 2 and above are Abair é, so after two right rewrites a line is only ever recalled aloud. Drop the odd and even page rule; item 4 is Líne nua whenever the pace needs it, else Abair é. Pair questions that are natural follow-ups (Q011 with Q012, Q020 with Q021, every 'Cad chuige?' with the question before it) so Abair é and the cold exam ask the pair in sequence, the way the examiner will. Athscríobh marks only the listed content words in the saved line, not word order or function words, so a paraphrase in good Irish is not marked as missing.

problems.problem: Athscríobh treats the pupil's own earlier line as the key. Nothing in the app can tell that the earlier line is good Irish, so twenty nights of rewriting from memory cements 'is maith liom ag imirt peile' and 'tá mé bhí' as firmly as the right forms. The printed page to the teacher is named as the correction route but there is no return route: a correction the teacher writes on paper never reaches the script.
problems.fix: Give every printed line a blank rule beneath it for the teacher's correction. In LineView add a draft type 'ceartú an mhúinteora' that the pupil enters after class; from then on that draft is the key for Athscríobh and Abair é, and the diagnosis category (fada, séimhiú, urú, briathar, focal) is chosen with one tap and goes into Mo chuid botún. A line's box cannot pass 2 until the page it sits on has been printed once, so the habit is not blocked but the teacher's eye is forced before a line is 'theirs'. The closing stamp names it when due: 'taispeáin an leathanach seo do do mhúinteoir'.

problems.problem: lineMark puts a grey ? on every word not found in the stage list after stripping mutations. The list holds headwords and verb roots; a good line is full of inflected forms (imrím, d'imir mé, rachaidh mé, cairde, scoile, deartháireacha) and proper nouns (Bessbrook, Ard Mhacha, Cumann Naomh Pól). A Higher line comes back peppered with question marks the pupil reads as wrong, and a pupil with ADHD reads as a wall of doubt. A teacher would not write ? on imrím.
problems.fix: Ticks only on the rules. The pen writes nothing about an unlisted word; ? appears only when the pupil taps a word, and that tap is what adds it to Mo chuid focal féin. If ? must be automatic, limit it to lower-case words that survive a small inflection strip (endings -im, -ann, -faidh, -fidh, -ann, -e, -a, -í, -anna, -acha; past d' and lenition; the verbal-noun ag form) and cap it at one per line.

problems.problem: The Barúlacha rule fires 'cad chuige?' on any opinion phrase with no mar. 'Mar' is also 'as' (mar mhúinteoir), and the Ulster reasons the department teaches are cionn is go, as siocair go, mar gheall ar, de bhrí go, óir. The pen would nag a pupil who gave a reason in the school's own idiom.
problems.fix: Fire 'cad chuige?' only on lines answering the 39 questions that ask for an opinion or reason (the ones containing Cad chuige, An maith leat, Cé acu is fearr, do bharúil, Ar mhaith leat), and accept mar, mar gheall ar, cionn is, as siocair, de bhrí, óir, toisc as a reason. Add the one diagnosis worth more marks than any of these: 'is maith liom ag imirt' gets the pen 'peil a imirt, nó bheith ag imirt peile', built from the 343 verbs with verbal nouns already in the data.

problems.problem: The GCSE list has 827 nouns and every one is marked m; feminine nouns sit in the 1,406 entries typed 'word'. So for a Year 11 or 12 pupil item 3 Foirm can only ever drill masculine nouns, the article drill will never produce an bhean or an tseachtain, and a feminine noun in the pupil's line is not recognised as a noun at all, so the mutation note after ar an, sa, leis an never fires on it.
problems.fix: Until the cleaning workbook replaces vocab.json, Foirm for Years 11 and 12 drills preposition plus article only, which in Ulster is gender-blind for b c f g m p, and the article drill runs only on the 362 gendered Key Stage 3 nouns. State this in the README as a known limit. The cleaning pass has to type every feminine entry as noun with gender f before the article drill is switched on for GCSE.

problems.problem: The mutation engine is wrong for Ulster on s. Mutate.prepArticle leaves s untouched, so it expects 'ag an siopa', 'sa seachtain', 'ar an sráid' and would mark 'ag an tsiopa', 'sa tseachtain', 'ar an tsráid' as wrong. The department teaches t before s after preposition and article (obligatory for feminine s plus vowel, l, n, r; usual in Ulster for masculine too), and the rule text in Grammar.swift ('ní athraíonn d, t ná s') would be read out by the pen as the school's position. Also 'fán' (Ulster faoin) is not in the accepted forms.
problems.fix: prepArticle prefixes t to s followed by a vowel, l, n or r: always for feminine, and for masculine by department ruling (accept both until the named teacher rules). Add fán as the accepted Ulster spelling of faoin. Delete the 'féach an riail' fallback diagnosis; if the engine cannot diagnose, the pen writes nothing. Every rule string is signed off by the named teacher before the pen can write it.

problems.problem: The 270 questions are GCSE speaking questions, most for Higher tier, and the brief puts Years 8 to 10 on the same script. A Year 8 cannot write a line on 'Cad iad na buntáistí/míbhuntáistí a bhaineann le...' and has no exam for four years, so 'Faoi lá an scrúdaithe' and the exam-date pace are false for them. The framework's named grammar (prepositional pronouns, verbs in positive, negative and question form) and phonics (62 correspondences) are absent; Foirm covers article and preposition mutation only.
problems.fix: Tag each of the 270 questions by tier and register (factual, descriptive, opinion) in the authoring pass alongside the English gloss, and let Líne nua take the next factual line for Foundation and Key Stage 3 pupils. For Years 8 to 10 the 'exam' on the cover is the end-of-year scrúdú béil the teacher sets, and their pages are the twelve topics limited to factual lines. Give Key Stage 3 Foirm a second engine over the pupil's own line: turn the verb negative or into a question (Tá mé to Níl mé and An bhfuil mé, regular past to Níor, future to Ní), and ag plus mé to agam using the 29 pppn rows. Phonics stays out until Abair audio exists; say so.

problems.problem: Focal (item 2) is bottomless and untethered. 'A word from the current page's list not yet in any line' draws on Caitheamh aimsire (316 entries) plus Dialann an lae (41) for the free-time page; a pupil would never exhaust it and none of it is guaranteed to be asked. The brief does not say what the pupil does with a Focal (type the Irish from English?), which is the flashcard the principal has already rejected, now on a rule.
problems.fix: Focal draws first from words the pen marked missing in tonight's Athscríobh, then from the words in the unwritten questions on the current topic page (deartháir, deirfiúr, teaghlach, cara, meas: folded headword match against the list), so the pupil meets the question's own vocabulary the night before the question. The pupil writes the word in a sentence of their own on the rule, not a translation; the pen ticks the word if it appears, mutation stripped. That keeps every rule as biro and feeds the script.

problems.problem: 'Leathanach' means two things: tonight's page (odd and even nights) and the twelve topic pages (Líne 12 de 21). A pupil with ADHD reading 'Leathanach eile' at the foot cannot tell whether that turns the night or the topic. And box 0 (0 days) makes a line written at item 4 tonight due for Athscríobh at item 1 tomorrow and, on an even night, also for Abair é at item 4: the same line twice in one page.
problems.fix: Call the night oíche (Oíche 7 in the stamp) and keep leathanach for the topic page only; the foot link is 'Oíche eile'. Rule: item 4 never takes the line item 1 just took. Persist each item as it closes, not the page, so a page abandoned after two items still keeps what was written.

problems.problem: Cúig bhomaite is promised. Athscríobh of a three-sentence line, a Focal, a Foirm, one to three new sentences typed with fadas on a phone, then Ceartúcháin, is six to eight minutes for a Higher pupil and longer for a Foundation pupil; 'anything crossed is written out again' can add three more rules. The 45-second wait before a hint is long for a pupil staring at a blank rule.
problems.fix: Cap Ceartúcháin at one form per night (the brief's own example shows one). Foundation and Key Stage 3 lines are one sentence. Hint after 20 seconds and make it the first word, not the first letter. Measure the real time on the first class and change the number on the cover, or drop the number and keep 'Leathanach amháin san oíche, sin an méid'.

problems.problem: The contents page of An scríbhinn shows twelve pages with counts (39, 36, 33...) and the Innéacs shows a topic's whole list with ticks: for a new pupil that is 270 blank lines and 2,200 unticked words, the queue the brief says is never shown. 'Never 270' in the candidate box is undone one tap away.
problems.fix: The contents page lists only the pages ticked on the cover, each as 'x de 21 scríofa'; the others sit in grey with no count until ticked. The Innéacs opens on the current topic page's list only, and for Key Stage 3 on the band the teacher sets, with the words already met listed first. The pace line surfaces when the ticked pages cannot be finished at one line a night before the exam month.

problems.problem: Mo chuid botún groups forms under 'ainm briathartha', but no item in the brief diagnoses verbal nouns; Grammar.swift emits only urú, séimhiú de dhíth, gan séimhiú anseo, t- de dhíth, t roimh s and féach an riail. A heading with nothing under it is decoration in the hand.
problems.fix: Either drop the heading or earn it with the 'is maith liom ag' diagnosis above and a verb-plus-verbal-noun check when a listed verb appears after ag in the pupil's line (ag imirt, not ag imir). Group only what the pen actually writes.

problems.problem: The blank-slot questions (Q093, Q094, Q101 to Q106) are filled from townland or club, but 'i(n) __' needs the locative form the engine cannot make (i gCamlach, in Ard Mhacha, sa tSruthán for Bessbrook, i mBaile Loch), and the twelve page titles exist only in English from the specification, which the app must not echo.
problems.fix: On the cover ask for the townland as the pupil says it after 'Tá mé i mo chónaí...' (i gCamlach, sa tSruthán), and use that string verbatim in Q104 and Q105; ask for the club the same way after 'Imrím le...'. Author twelve Irish page titles (Mé féin, mo theaghlach, caidrimh agus roghanna; Caitheamh aimsire agus an gnáthlá; and so on) and have the named teacher sign them with the 270 glosses.

critiques.stillMissing: Three things a pupil still cannot learn from the app itself. First, what the exam is: the brief never says it is a conversation with a teacher-examiner, so a pupil sees a booklet and concludes this is for the writing paper; one line under the cover's exam date (Comhrá deich mbomaite le scrúdaitheoir, ar dhá ábhar a roghnaíonn tú) would fix it. Second, what happens to the page: whether a teacher ever sees it, and how their correction gets back in; the pupil should be told on the cover that the printed page is for the teacher and that the teacher's correction becomes the line. Third, for Years 8 to 10, what they are building towards at all, since 'lá an scrúdaithe' is four years away; the cover for those years must name the end-of-year scrúdú béil and the framework's own promise, that they will speak without preparation, as the point. Until the gloss and tier tag exist on the 270 questions, a Foundation pupil also cannot tell which lines are theirs to write and which are beyond them.

critiques.lens: Product designer who has seen a thousand language apps: does one idea run through every screen, and is the exam-script register doing work or decorating?

problems.problem: The word-by-word marking of a new line (item 4, Líne nua) cannot be delivered by the data and will read as failure. Against the GCSE list in vocab.json an ordinary correct Year 11 line, 'Tá deartháir amháin agam agus tá sé níos sine ná mé, imrím peil leis ag an deireadh seachtaine, is maith liom é mar bíonn craic againn', gets a grey ? on tá, agam, níos, sine, imrím, leis, an, sa, is, maith, liom, é, bíonn and againn: 15 of 29 words. Adding the frequency list still leaves sine, imrím and seachtaine unmatched because the lists hold headwords, not genitives, comparatives or conjugated verbs. A pupil with ADHD does not read 'grey means unlisted'; they read a line covered in question marks as wrong. The Index then fills with ? noise and the Focal picker draws on it.
problems.fix: The pen marks only what it can check, and never per word. On a new line the pen writes at most three things: fada! where a diacritic-folded match exists, a mutation note after the nine prepositions where the noun's gender is known, and cad chuige? after an opinion phrase with no mar. Listed-word recognition goes to the Index only (a small print tick beside the word, not the pen), looked up against both lists plus a stop list of function words and inflections. The ? disappears as a mark; a tap-to-add-to-Mo-chuid-focal-féin affordance is a faint dotted underline in print, not red, not the hand.

problems.problem: Foirm (item 3) will mark correct Irish wrong in the principal's hand for every Year 11 and 12 pupil until the cleaning workbook lands. In vocab.json all 827 GCSE nouns carry gender 'm' (the source marks only masculine; feminine is the absence of a tag, and the extraction wrote 'm' on everything). Removing 'noun.gender ?? "m"' does nothing here because the value is not nil, it is wrong. 'an + fuinneog' would be expected as 'an fuinneog' and 'an fhuinneog' crossed out in red. The frequency list is clean (236 n (m), 113 n (f)).
problems.fix: Until the workbook replaces vocab.json, Foirm takes gender only from the frequency list rows (pos 'n (m)' or 'n (f)'), matched by folded headword to the noun in the pupil's line; a GCSE-only noun has unknown gender and is never drilled. Add a genderVerified flag to VocabItem so the workbook can switch this on per row. State this limit in README.md.

problems.problem: The purpose collapses for Years 8 to 10. The script is 270 examiner questions; the first-open copy speaks of 'an scrúdaitheoir' and 'lá an scrúdaithe'; the candidate box carries an exam month; the pace is exam-driven. A Year 8 pupil has no examiner, no exam month, and no reason to write 'Cad é an rud is mó a thaitníonn leat faoi Bhéal Feirste' on line 106. The brief derives the frequency list from yearGroup 8 to 10 but never says what those pupils write lines about, so for them the thread does not exist.
problems.fix: Scope this app to Years 11 and 12 (Rang 11 or 12 on the inside cover, nothing else offered). Keep the frequency list on board only as the clean gender and lookup source. A Key Stage 3 booklet is a second object (the 29 Nathanna coitianta and the phonics words as its lines) and gets its own brief when the 2028 framework settles.

problems.problem: Nights 2 and 3 are four repetitions of 'Aoife is ainm dom'. The first page has item 4 only (line 1, Cad é an t-ainm atá ort?). On night 2 a box-0 line is due, so Athscríobh is L1, Focal is a word missed in L1 or a page word, Foirm is a noun from L1 (ainm), Abair é is L1. The pupil who most needs the first week to land gets the emptiest week. The inside cover also asks for name, class and townland, which are lines 1, 2, 6 and 7 asked again.
problems.fix: Night 1 is the inside cover and lines 1 to 7 together: the seven short opening questions of page 1 (name, where you live, family, brothers, sisters, school, class) are written as one item in biro, the way a candidate fills the front of a script. The inside cover pre-fills nothing on a rule; the pupil types each. Athscríobh, Focal and Foirm then have seven lines to draw on from night 2.

problems.problem: Two things are called a page and they disagree on every screen. 'Leathanach an lae' is a night; 'Líne 12 de 21' and 'twelve topic pages' are the script; 'odd pages Líne nua, even pages Abair é' counts nights; 'Leathanach eile' at the foot opens a second night on the same night. The first-open copy says 'líonfaidh tú leathanach amháin' every night, and the pupil then sees a page they will take 42 nights to fill. Line references 'L12' are ambiguous across twelve pages of 9 to 39 lines each.
problems.fix: A page is a topic page and nothing else. The nightly unit is Anocht (rubric unchanged, Do scrúdú, scríofa agat roimh ré). Odd and even nights, not pages; 'Tuilleadh anocht' replaces Leathanach eile. Every line reference carries page and line in print, '1.12' or 'lch 1, L12', including in the closing stamp and the Index. First-open copy: 'Achan oíche, ceithre rud, cúig bhomaite.'

problems.problem: The pen makes wrong Irish permanent. With no model answers, the pupil's own first draft is the key for Athscríobh; a line with a wrong verb form is rewritten, ticked by the pen for matching itself, and pushed to a 16-day box in the principal's red hand. The brief admits 'the app cannot say a line is good Irish' and offers the printed page as the correction route, but there is no route for the teacher's corrections to come back into the script, and a per-word tick is not a thing any teacher writes; it is a gamification skin wearing a pen.
problems.fix: Add the return leg. The printed page carries a tick box per line for the teacher. In LineView a 'Ceartaithe ag an mhúinteoir' action lets the pupil enter the teacher's corrected line as a new draft dated and marked 'múinteoir' in small print; the old draft is struck through. Until a line has that mark, its Leitner box caps at 2 (four days) and the margin shows 'gan seiceáil' in print. The pen's tick on Athscríobh means only 'you remembered your own line' and says so in the rubric: 'Athscríobh líne 4 ó chuimhne.'

problems.problem: The single Athscríobh slot cannot service the queue, so the boxes are decoration. A candidate's two conversation topics are about 60 lines. At steady state a line in the 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 ladder needs a rewrite roughly every ten days: six due lines a night against one slot. 'The queue is never shown' hides a backlog that grows from about week eight, and the pace warning cannot fire because the four-item structure cannot exceed half a line a night while Líne nua alternates with Abair é.
problems.fix: Retire lines: a line that clears box 5 is 'agat' and appears only in Abair é and the cold exam. Let both Athscríobh and Abair é advance a line's box, and let Abair é choose the most overdue line. Pace drives the rhythm: when unwritten lines on the ticked pages divided by school nights exceeds 0.5, every night is Líne nua and Abair é takes item 1's slot on even nights in place of Athscríobh. Print the arithmetic in README.md.

problems.problem: Focal (b), 'a word from the current page's list not yet in any line', turns the app back into the 2,200-word drill the principal rejected. Page 2 (Free time) maps to Caitheamh aimsire and Dialann an lae, 357 words, for 39 lines. The pupil is shown an English word with no connection to anything they wrote, on a rule, which fails the print test: no exam script carries a translation item. The Index rubric 'Na focail atá de dhíth ar do scríbhinn' then lists 300 words the pupil will never tick, a permanent record of absence for a pupil who needs a filling page.
problems.fix: Drop Focal (b). Focal draws only from words the pen marked missing in a rewrite and from due words; when there are none, the night has three items. Give Focal and Foirm the same exam shape, a gap in the pupil's own line: 'Tá ______ deartháir agam (one)' and 'Téim ar scoil sa ______ (carr)'. The Index lists only words that have appeared in a line, rubric 'Na focail atá i do scríbhinn'; the untouched remainder of the page list feeds the Líne nua word bank silently.

problems.problem: A stuck pupil on Líne nua has nowhere to go. Q019 'Déan cur síos ar dhuine a bhfuil meas agat air' with no model answer, no opener, and a first-letter hint that means nothing for free composition. This is the exact moment a pupil with ADHD closes the app, and the brief's only scaffold is a word bank of 27 opinion phrases and 30 connectives.
problems.fix: Author 270 openers instead of 270 model answers: the first three to five words of a plausible Ulster answer per question ('Tá mo chara is fearr ...', 'Is é mo dheartháir ...'), one line each, signed off by the named teacher. After 45 seconds idle the pen writes the opener in the margin. Add 'Fág go fóill' as a LinkButton: the rule stays blank, the next unwritten question comes up, no mark, no note. Keep the PROPOSAL's section D frames (is maith liom + ainm briathartha, ba mhaith liom + ..., is dóigh liom go ...) as the word bank's first row.

problems.problem: Forty-two of the 270 questions are not one question. Q051, Q056, Q071 and Q077 carry rinne/dhéanann/dhéanfaidh (three tenses); Q063 carries four alternatives and two time frames; Q040 'An maith leat an teilifís/spórt?'. Written as one numbered line they confuse on first open, and the tense alternatives are the grammar-for-meaning content the framework cares about most, thrown away by treating them as one line.
problems.fix: Resolve the slashes at data time, in the same pass that authors the English glosses. Tense alternatives become sub-lines (a), (b), (c) under one number, the way the papers set them; either/or alternatives are split or the first kept. questions.json gains 'part' and the count per page is recomputed before any 'Líne n de N' is shown.

problems.problem: The closing stamp is a score wearing a hat, and the pen writes things a teacher would not. '4 thic, ceartú amháin, Mé féin: 12 de 21' is a tally; the brief elsewhere says the closing comment is 'kind and about a named thing'. 'Mé féin' also names a topic page, but questions.json topics are in English ('Myself, my family, relationships and choices') and the brief never lists the twelve Irish page titles.
problems.fix: The stamp names the work: the date, then one line about one thing ('L4 ó chuimhne. sa charr ceartaithe.'), then 'Sin é anocht.' No counts. Author and sign off twelve short Irish page titles (for example Mé féin agus mo theaghlach; Caitheamh aimsire agus an gnáthlá; Na meáin shóisialta agus an teicneolaíocht; Nósanna agus féilte; Mo cheantar; An timpeallacht; Cúrsaí sóisialta; Taisteal; Mo chuid oibre scoile; Imeachtaí iarscoile; Obair pháirtaimseartha agus airgead; Pleanáil don todhchaí) and carry them in questions.json.

problems.problem: Athscríobh punishes improvement. The rewrite is marked against the saved line, so a pupil who writes a better second version gets the earlier word in red as 'missing'. Abair é overwrites the only recording per question id, so the original said line is lost each time.
problems.fix: In rewriteMark only listed words from the saved line that are absent count as missing; new listed words are ignored. After marking, offer 'Coinnigh an ceann seo' to adopt the rewrite as the current draft, the earlier draft struck through and dated. Name recordings by question id and date; keep the first and the latest.

problems.problem: The cold exam promises 'Mar a bheas sé ar an lá' with the question shown in print and no voice. On the day the examiner speaks. Until Abair exists the rubric overclaims, and the 27 Barúlacha phrases used to trigger cad chuige? include 'dom', 'mar', 'áfach', 'b'fhéidir' and 'ina áit sin', so 'Aoife is ainm dom' on line 1 draws cad chuige? from the pen.
problems.fix: Rubric until audio lands: 'Cúig cheist, gan do scríbhinn os do chomhair.' Restrict the cad chuige? trigger to the thirteen opinion frames (is maith liom, ní maith liom, is breá liom, is fearr liom, is fuath liom, is aoibhinn liom, is grá liom, tá dúil agam i, sílim go, is dóigh liom go, is é mo bharúil go, cuireann sé isteach orm, níl suim dá laghad agam ann).

problems.problem: Small register breaks that would each fail the print test or the hand: Mo chuid botún promises an 'ainm briathartha' group but Grammar.swift diagnoses only urú, séimhiú, t- and ts; the hand has no apostrophe yet Irish corrections need one (m'athair, d'am, b'fhéidir) and a pupil's name may too; the foot must carry one action yet tonight's page also carries the contents line; and the first-open copy says 'Marcálfaidh mise é' without telling the pupil whose hand it is or that the marking is automatic, which for a pupil at this school is either a thrill or a threat.
problems.fix: Either add a verbal-noun check (a word after 'ag' must match a vn field) or drop the group. Digitise the apostrophe and the capital fadas from the sample sheet. Put the contents line above the foot as a printed running foot in grey ('An scríbhinn · Innéacs · Clúdach istigh'), the foot itself keeps one action. First-open gains one print sentence: the marking is automatic, in the hand of Dáithí Murray, and your teacher sees the printed page.

critiques.stillMissing: On first open the brief tells the pupil what the app is for in ninety words of Irish, which is the one thing a pupil who cannot yet write a line of Irish cannot read. What is still missing is the object itself, shown before it is explained: one finished page of a script (a specimen, in biro, red marks in the margin, Críochnaithe across it, dated) with a single print line, 'Seo mar a bheas do leathanach féin faoi Bhealtaine'. The brief also never tells the pupil how much of the script is theirs: the speaking exam draws on two conversation topics, so a candidate's script is about 60 lines on two pages, not 270 on twelve, and that number is the one that makes 'five minutes a night until May' believable. Finally the brief does not say what the teacher does with the printed page, so the pupil cannot see why a line that the pen ticked might still need to change.

revised.purpose: Write your own answers to the examiner's questions, one line a night, until nothing in the conversation is new.
revised.brief:
# Mo Scríbhinn

## What it is for

Write your own answers to the examiner's questions, one line a night, until nothing in the conversation is new.

After twenty school nights: twenty lines in biro on the two chosen pages, the first sheet finished, each line rewritten from memory and said aloud, one printed sheet back from the teacher with a correction typed in.

## The thread

The script. One exam booklet belonging to one candidate, and it is the data structure, not a skin: the candidate's two conversation topics as pages, each cut into sheets of ten to twenty numbered lines. A line is the pupil's own answer to one question, in biro, marked in the Principal's red hand for what a machine can check, printed for the teacher who corrects the rest, rewritten and later said from memory until it is theirs.

On every screen: the candidate box carries Ainm, Rang, Scrúdú (Bealtaine 2028) and the standing on the current sheet (Líne 5 de 11), never a score; the italic rubric with its English beneath is the only heading; each item has a print instruction; a rule carries only biro; the margin carries line references in print and marks in the hand; one action at the foot, a grey running foot naming the other pages; no tab bar.

## First open

The inside cover, filled in as a candidate fills a real one: Ainm, Rang (11 or 12), Scrúdú, two topic pages ticked, townland as said after Tá mé i mo chónaí, club as said after Imrím le. Then the first sheet, blank, its questions printed on the rules: the object before the paragraph. The cover's text is permanent.

Irish: Seo do scríbhinn féin. Ar na leathanaigh seo tá na ceisteanna a chuirfeas an scrúdaitheoir ort sa chomhrá, agus do chuid freagraí féin orthu. Achan oíche: líne amháin nua i do chuid focal féin, agus líne a scríobh tú cheana, ó chuimhne. Ceartóidh an peann dearg na fadaí, an séimhiú agus an t-urú; is í an aip a mharcálann, i lámh an Phríomhoide. Do mhúinteoir a cheartóidh an chuid eile, ón leathanach a phriontálann tú. Faoi lá an scrúdaithe ní bheidh rud ar bith le rá agat den chéad uair.

English: This is your own exam script. On these pages are the questions the examiner will ask you in the conversation, and your own answers to them. Every night: one new line in your own words, and one line you wrote before, from memory. The red pen corrects fadas, séimhiú and urú; the app does the marking, in the Principal's hand. Your teacher corrects the rest, from the page you print. By exam day there will be nothing you have to say for the first time.

## Home

No home apart from the work: the app opens on Anocht; leathanach means a topic page only. Every night the rubric reads Do scrúdú, scríofa agat roimh ré, English beneath; then the standing and item 1 live. The one action: write on the live rule. Night one has one item: the seven one-sentence questions at the top of the first sheet, written together.

## The screens

**1. Anocht.** Four items, fixed order, one live. 1 Ó chuimhne, the most overdue line, never two: in box 0 or 1 Athscríobh, from memory, marked only on listed words missing from the saved line; from box 2 Abair é, sheet face down, recorded, played back against the revealed line. 2 Focal: a word missed in item 1, else a listed word from the next question, in the pupil's own sentence. 3 Foirm: a gap in the pupil's own line, Téim ar scoil sa ______ (carr), diagnosed by rule. 4 Líne nua: the next question. The pen writes at most three things: fada!, a mutation note where the noun's gender is known, cad chuige? on an opinion question without a reason word, bheith ag after a bare is maith liom ag; never per-word ticks or question marks. The opener in grey print after twenty seconds idle; Fág go fóill skips. Ceartúcháin: one form, once. Close: the date, one kind line about one thing, Sin é anocht.

**2. An scríbhinn.** Rubric: Gach a ndéarfaidh tú ar lá an scrúdaithe. The two ticked pages and their sheets, the rest grey; lines in biro with date, taifeadta, le seiceáil until printed; Críochnaithe across a finished sheet; Priontáil an leathanach; Scrúdú béil once finished.

**3. Líne.** Rubric: the question. Drafts crossed through and dated, recordings, word bank, Athscríobh ó chuimhne, Ceartú an mhúinteora: the teacher's correction typed in becomes the key, one tap naming the fault.

**4. Innéacs.** Rubric: Na focail atá i do scríbhinn. Only words already in a line, by sheet, gender where known, line reference; then Mo chuid focal féin and Mo chuid botún in the hand.

**5. Scrúdú béil.** Rubric: Cúig cheist, gan do scríbhinn os do chomhair. From a finished sheet, pairs in sequence, the question in the teacher's voice, print on a second tap, the only countdown, tic or arís.

**6. An clúdach istigh.** Rubric: Cé thú féin agus cá huair a bheas an scrúdú. The candidate details, the text above, a print line that the exam is a conversation on two chosen topics, Priontáil an scríbhinn ar fad, Glan.

## A school night in five minutes

Aoife, 11B, sheet 1b, Líne 5 de 11. Item 1, Athscríobh 1a.4, Cá mhéad deartháir atá agat?: she leaves out amháin; the pen writes amháin de dhíth. Item 2: amháin in her own sentence, tic. Item 3, sa ______ (carr) from her own 1a.2: she types carr; crossed, charr above, séimhiú de dhíth. Item 4, Cad é mar a réitíonn tú le do chlann?: Réitím go maith le mo chlann. Is maith liom ag caint le mo mhamaí mar tá sí greannmhar. The pen writes bheith ag caint. Ceartúcháin: sa charr once. The stamp: the date, sa charr ceartaithe, maith thú, Sin é anocht.

## The exam-script register, what it must do

Keep it. The test for every screen: could it be printed and handed to a teacher as a page of a candidate's script. The pen writes only what a teacher could check and would write; the printed sheet carries a blank rule under each line and a tick box for the teacher's real red pen. It fails the moment the pen ticks what it cannot judge.

## For a pupil with ADHD

Progress is an object that fills inside a fortnight: a sheet, Críochnaithe across it. The same four items in the same order every night, one live; the queue never shown; the count is the current sheet. Marking is instant; one wrong form is written out again before the night closes. Boxes of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 days, a line moving from paper to voice after two right rewrites. No streak, no timer except the cold exam.

## What comes out of the current build

The TabView. HomeView's statistics, streak and maith tick. The score slot in ExamHeader. The Aonad labels. GrammarView, its rule box, féach an riail and the gender default of m. SettingsView's Form and stage picker. Intervals 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 30. From the last brief: per-word ticks and the grey ?, odd and even pages, Focal from the whole list, the tally in the stamp, leathanach for a night, Years 8 to 10. The name Cuimhne.

## What has to be true before it can be built

Data: a twelve-row topic table with Irish page titles, vocabulary groups and sheet cuts; the 270 questions each with English gloss, tier, register, follow-up pair and a three to five word opener, the 42 slash questions resolved, Q093 and Q094 authored; the topic list's gender cleaned in the workbook, until which Foirm drills the article only on the 362 gendered frequency-list nouns; an apostrophe and capital fadas digitised from the sample sheet; every Irish string signed off by a named teacher. Audio: the 270 questions recorded by a teacher on a phone before the cold exam may claim to be like the day. Model answers: none; the pupil's line is the key, the teacher's correction replaces it, the openers stand in. Years 11 and 12 only; Key Stage 3 is a second booklet.

Extend questions.json with en (gloss), pageGa (Irish page title), sheet (1a, 1b), part (a, b, c for tense alternatives), tier, register (factual, descriptive, opinion), pair (follow-up question id) and opener; add a twelve-row topic table from questions.json topic to vocab.json groups and sheet cuts (Free time into 3 sheets, Local area, School and Part-time into 2 each).
